Introduction  Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains the leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide [ 1 ]. Platinum-based chemoimmunotherapy combining cytotoxic agents with immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) has extended survival in some patients and is standard both as a neoadjuvant setting and a first-line treatment for advanced disease [ 2 – 5 ]. Despite ongoing real-world data analyses, reliable biomarkers capable of definitively distinguishing durable responders from non-responders are needed [ 6 ,  7 ].  The presence and maturity of tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) within the tumor microenvironment have emerged as key prognostic and predictive elements across multiple solid tumors [ 8 – 10 ]. In NSCLC, the densities of DC-LAMP⁺ mature dendritic cells and CD20⁺ B cells within TLSs are correlated with long-term survival [ 11 ,  12 ]. Mature TLSs are linked to favorable ICI response in various types of cancers, such as NSCLC and bladder cancer, and then high levels of intra-tumoral CXCL13 expression mark patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer likely to respond to treatment [ 13 ,  14 ].  The canonical 12-chemokine “TLS gene signature” is employed to predict TLS regions in transcriptomic analyses [ 15 ,  16 ]. However, its expression varies across tumor types, underscoring the inter-cancer TLS heterogeneity and the need for more tumor-specific functional TLS markers [ 17 ]. Our re-analysis of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data to isolate TLS-like cells with the 12-chemokine scores yielded few B-cell populations in breast ( n  = 26) and lung ( n  = 185) cancer samples (Supplementary Fig. S1A, B) [ 18 ,  19 ], highlighting the limitations of dissociative single-cell methods for analyzing structured niches. Therefore, spatially resolved transcriptomics is essential for capturing TLS architecture and heterogeneity in situ.  Previous studies have investigated spatial transcriptomics focused on TLS [ 20 – 22 ]. Immature TLSs enriched with immunosuppressive macrophages and regulatory T cells confer resistance to ICB, particularly in peritoneal metastases in gastric cancer [ 23 ]. Additionally, tumors containing mature TLSs can exhibit primary ICB resistance driven by distinct cancer-associated fibroblast subsets (FAP⁺ αSMA⁺ and MYH11⁺ αSMA⁺) in NSCLC [ 24 ]. Collectively, these studies demonstrated the effects of both TLS maturity and cellular composition on therapeutic outcomes. However, to date, the spatiotemporal dynamics of endothelial cells within TLSs have not been assessed using single-cell resolution methods.  Therefore, the present study applied high-resolution Xenium In Situ spatial single-cell transcriptomics to resected NSCLC specimens. We investigated the cellular components, endothelial cell dynamics, and cell–cell interactions within TLS associated region by TLS maturity and treatment status with or without chemo-immunotherapy. The study design is shown in Fig.  1 . The resulting dataset provides a foundational atlas of TLS regions in NSCLC and highlights inhibitor of DNA binding 1 (ID1)-high endothelial venules (HEVs) as a potential biomarker, offering insights to guide new immunotherapeutic approaches or enhance the effectiveness of current treatments.    Fig. 1   Study design and cohorts. ( A ) Xenium discovery cohort: profiling of eight resected NSCLC specimens (four neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy, four untreated) using spatial single-cell transcriptomics allowed the manual annotation of 90 TLS regions for downstream analyses. ( B ) Biomarker validation cohort: 45 archival NSCLC resections from patients treated with immune-checkpoint blockade after recurrence were interrogated by multiplex immunofluorescence for TLS/HEV markers and linked to overall patient survival                     Materials and methods   Patients and samples  Tissue specimens and clinical records from patients with NSCLC were collected at 14 Japanese institutions between January 2017 and February 2024. Consistent with the KEYNOTE-189, CheckMate-816, and CheckMate-9LA protocols [ 2 ,  4 ,  5 ], patients harboring major EGFR mutations or ALK rearrangements were excluded.  In the xenium discovery cohort, we initially identified 29 patients who underwent surgical resection within the preceding two years, with or without neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy. Patients who achieved clinical complete response after the neoadjuvant therapy or received perioperative radiotherapy were excluded. Furthermore, we selected eight patients showing TLSs enrichment in immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis (as described below) and with an RNA DV200 ≥ 30%. Given the limited tissue from pre-treatment bronchoscopic biopsies, matched pre-/post-treatment pairs were not available, and independent resected specimens were used for Xenium analysis. Therefore, the final analysis included four patients who received neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy and four patients who underwent surgery without neoadjuvant chemotherapy, analyzed as independent patient samples (Supplementary Fig. S2A, B). In the biomarker validation cohort using multiplex-immunofluorescence (MIF), 683 patients who underwent ICB with or without chemotherapy were initially screened. Among these, 575 patients were excluded because the available specimens were derived from bronchoscopy, metastatic-site biopsy, computed tomography-guided needle biopsy, or because no residual tissue remained. Archived lung specimens obtained prior to any immunotherapy exposure were available from 108 surgical cases. Among these, 45 patients who later initiated immunotherapy within two years after postoperative recurrence were enrolled for MIF (as described below), and survival analysis (Supplementary Fig. S3).  Additionally, we retrieved a scRNA-seq dataset comprising 26 breast cancer specimens from the GEO (accession  GSE176078 ) and downloaded an integrated scRNA-seq dataset of 185 NSCLC specimens from Figshare (DOI: 10.6084/m9.figshare.c.6222221.v3).    Treatment responses and survival evaluation  Clinical variables, including age, sex, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status, smoking history, histology, programmed death-ligand 1 tumor proportion score (PD-L1 TPS), clinical stage, and treatment outcomes, were extracted from patient records. PD-L1 TPS was measured with the 22C3 antibody. Radiographic responses were categorized according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors v1.1 [ 25 ]. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the time from chemo-immunotherapy initiation to death or the last follow-up. The data cut-off date was March 31, 2025.    IHC and MIF examination  Chromogenic IHC was performed on 5 μm formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) lung-cancer sections after Tris-EDTA retrieval (pH 9.0, 95 °C, 40 min) and peroxidase quenching (Dako REAL). Serial sections were incubated at 4 °C overnight with primary antibodies including anti-CD3 (Proteintech, #60181-1-Ig, 1:800), anti-CD20 (Proteintech, #60271-1-Ig, 1:1000), and anti-PNAd (BioLegend, clone MECA-79, #120801, 1:100). Detection was performed using an HRP–DAB system following the manufacturers’ instructions. MIF was performed with two four-marker panels. Panel 1: CD20 (Abcam, #ab194970, 1:200), CD23-CL594 (Proteintech, clone 4C7C9, #CL594-60208-2, 1:100), CD3-CL647 (Proteintech, clone 3F3A1, #CL647-60181, 1:100), and CXCL12 (CST, clone D8G6H, #97958, 1:100); Panel 2: MECA-79-AF488 (Invitrogen, clone MECA-79, #53-6-36–82, 1:50), CD31 (Proteintech, clone 3F8E2, #66065-2-Ig, 1:100), CD20 (Abcam, #ab194970, 1:200), and ID1 (CST, clone F2M1J, #23369, 1:100).  Fluorescence was detected using the following secondary antibodies: donkey anti-goat Alexa Fluor 488, donkey anti-goat Alexa Fluor 647, donkey anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 594 (Invitrogen, 1:500, 1 h, room temperature), and goat anti-rabbit CoraLite Plus 750 (Proteintech, 1:200, 1 h, RT). The slides were mounted in antifade medium with DAPI (Invitrogen) and imaged on an FV3000 confocal microscope (Olympus) with 20×, 40×, and 60× objectives under identical laser and gain settings.    IHC quantification  TLSs were identified with a two-step procedure as previously described [ 26 ]. First, serial sections were immunostained for CD20 (B cells), CD3 (T cells), and PNAd (HEV). TLS-positive specimens showed clusters of T cells surrounding aggregates of B cells. Second, TLSs were divided into three status by B-cell density and follicular architecture: absent, immature, and mature. CXCL12 protein level was quantified using ImageJ (v 2.9.0/1.53t) as the mean percentage of the TLS area with positive staining in three representative fields. Cases above and below the cohort median (excluding TLS-negative samples) were classified as CXCL12-high and CXCL12-low, respectively. ID1 status was determined by counting ID1-positive endothelial cells in HEVs within TLSs across three representative microscopic fields. Specimens with a mean count ≥ 10 and < 10 cells were classified as ID1-high and ID1-low, respectively. Two investigators trained in digital histopathology reviewed the images independently and were blinded to the clinical data. Discrepancies were resolved by joint review, and the final status was verified by an additional pathologist.    Xenium in situ workflow  Five-micron FFPE sections (DV200 ≥ 30%) containing TLSs by IHC were processed using the Xenium FFPE workflow (see 10x Genomics,  CG000601  Rev B). After de-paraffinization, decrosslinking, and Tris-EDTA retrieval, the slides were hybridized overnight at 50 °C with a 430-gene probe set (10 nM each, 380-gene Human Immune-Oncology base panel plus 50 custom endothelial-focused custom genes; Supplementary Table S1), then ligated and amplified by rolling-circle amplification. The prepared slides were run on the Xenium Analyzer, which executed 15 automated cycles of fluorescent probe binding, imaging, and stripping, capturing 0.75 μm Z-stacks across the entire 12 × 24 mm imaging area. The on-instrument pipeline stitched fields of view, segmented nuclei/cells from DAPI, and decoded transcripts by maximum-likelihood matching to the gene codebook. Transcripts with calibrated Q-scores ≥ 20 were retained. A cell-by-gene count matrix, segmentation masks; and morphology images were exported for downstream analysis.    Xenium in situ analyses  Cell segmentation morphology images generated by the Xenium Analyzer were co-registered with the corresponding H&E images, after which every TLS was manually delineated, and the constituent cells were extracted for downstream analysis (Supplementary Fig. S4). TLS boundaries were drawn to encompass contiguous clusters of immune cells. All spatial transcriptomic analyses in this study were restricted to cells located within these manually annotated TLS regions of interest. Tumor parenchyma outside the TLS boundaries was not included in the expression matrices used for any downstream analyses.  All analyses were carried out using R software (v 4.4.2) and Python (v 3.12.9). Using Seurat package (v 5.2.1), we generated a separate Seurat object for each TLS and removed low-quality cells (< 5 detected genes and < 10 total transcript counts). All TLS objects were then pooled into a single Seurat object for downstream processing. Gene expression matrices were normalized using the NormalizeData function, variable features were identified with the FindVariableFeatures function, and linear scaling was applied using the ScaleData function. PCA was performed with the RunPCA function and the optimal number of principal components (PCs) was selected from the ElbowPlot. Batch effects arising from sample identity were corrected by applying the RunHarmony function to the PCA embeddings, and clustering was conducted on the Harmony-integrated PCs using the Louvain algorithm [ 27 ]. The same embeddings were used to generate Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) visualizations.  Because spatial transcriptomics can misassign transcripts to neighboring cells, the cell-type annotation did not rely solely on canonical markers. Rather, candidate markers for each cluster were identified using FindMarkers function (log fold-change > 0.20;  P  < 0.01), and the resulting labels were imported into Xenium Explorer, where they were cross-validated against cellular morphology and histological context (e.g., endothelial cells continuity). Higher-resolution analyses were performed for endothelial cells, with each population re-extracted into a new Seurat object, dimensional reduction and clustering repeated as described above, and cell-type identities refined (Supplementary Table S2) [ 15 ,  28 – 31 ]. Mixed clusters were similarly reclassified, and the final cell-type labels were appended to the metadata of the main object.  Differentially expressed genes were identified for each cell type with two-sided t-tests, with significance thresholds of |log₂ fold change| ≥ 0.20 and  P  < 0.01. Genes that met these criteria were subjected to Gene Ontology overrepresentation analysis to elucidate the biological pathways that were preferentially affected in each comparison. Cell–cell communications (CCIs) were reconstructed using CellChat package (v 2.1.2), which quantitatively infers ligand–receptor interaction networks from scRNA-seq profiles. To place these interactions in their spatial context, we subsequently analyzed the CCIs within each field of view, including TLSs, using stLearn (v 0.4.10).    Statistical analyses  Continuous variables and dichotomous variables are summarized as medians with inter-quartile ranges and absolute counts with percentages, respectively. Group differences in categorical data were assessed with Pearson’s χ² or Fisher’s exact tests, as appropriate. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to compare TLS counts and the cellular compositions stratified by TLS maturity and treatment arm. OS was evaluated using Kaplan–Meier curves (log-rank test) and modelled using Cox proportional-hazards regression. The independent correlates of TLS maturation and CXCL12/ID1 status were identified with multivariable logistic regression. All analyses were performed in R (v 4.4.2), and two-sided P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.     Results   Spatial single-cell atlas reveals B-cell-dominated TLS architecture independent of neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy  The eight-patient Xenium discovery cohort is summarized in Table  1 . Apart from a slightly younger median age in the ICB plus chemotherapy arm, the two groups were well balanced for sex, clinical stage, histological subtype and PD-L1 TPS. Neoadjuvant treatment produced one pathological complete response, with partial responses in the remaining cases. A density map from Xenium Explorer demonstrated that a composite oncogenic signature, based on  CEACAM6 ,  EGFR ,  EPCAM ,  ERBB2 ,  ERBB3 ,  MET ,  MUC5AC  and  TMPRSS2 , closely tracked with therapeutic efficacy. Moreover, serial sections confirmed PNAd-positive HEV in all TLSs (Supplementary Fig. S5). After filtering, 319,909 cells were retained and classified based on canonical markers into 16 cell-type clusters: conventional B cells (Bconv), follicular B cells (FoB), proliferating B cells, conventional CD4⁺ T cells (CD4_Tconv), follicular-helper T cells (Tfh), regulatory T cells (Treg), CD8⁺ T cells, plasma cells, macrophages, mature and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (mDC, pDC), mast cells, neutrophils, endothelial cells, fibroblasts and tumor cells (Fig.  2 A). Unintegrated UMAPs showed specimen-specific clustering; however, harmony correction merged cells from all eight samples into shared lineage islands, indicating effective removal of batch effects (Fig.  2 B). CXCR5  peaked in FoB and Tfh cells, whereas  FCER2  was highest in FoB and proliferating B cells.  CXCL13 , which is typically restricted to Tfh cells remained Tfh-dominant yet al.so appeared in a subset of B-cell clusters [ 32 ]. Additional markers confirmed cell-type specificity:  FOXP3  (Treg),  CD8A  (CD8⁺ T),  FKBP11  (plasma),  APOE  (macrophage),  IDO1  (mDC) and  CDH5  (endothelial) (Fig.  2 C). Overlaying these annotations on matched H&E images reproduced the classical TLS blueprint: FoB and proliferating B cells packed the germinal-center core; CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cells formed concentric mantles; and plasma, DCs and endothelial cells ringed the periphery (Fig.  2 D) [ 33 ].  The cellular composition was strikingly reproducible across patients. B-cell subsets dominated, with Bconv (18.5%) and FoB (17.6%) together comprising ~ 36%, and proliferating B cells adding 2.8%. T-cell populations accounted for ~ 33%: CD4_Tconv 17.7%, CD8⁺ T 11.4%, Tfh 2.2% and Treg 1.6%. Myeloid cells were less abundant (macrophages 4.5%, mDCs 1.0%), and each remaining cell-types, including endothelial and fibroblast cells, accounted for roughly 8% of the compartment (Fig.  2 E). Overall, spatial single-cell mapping yielded a reproducible B-cell-centered TLS atlas that was consistent across all samples.    TLS maturation reshapes immune niches and improves survival under cancer immunotherapy  To minimize therapy-related bias, TLS maturation was interrogated exclusively in untreated controls. Representative Xenium Explorer and MIF findings readily distinguished compact, mantle-ringed B-cell follicles from loosely organized, T-cell–rich aggregates, designating the former as mature and the latter as immature.  CXCL13 ,  CXCR5 ,  FCER2  and  MS4A1  were highly concentrated in mature cores; their combined expression was converted into a “mature-TLS score” with AddModuleScore function (Fig.  3 A) [ 34 ,  35 ]. Using a threshold of 0 separated 22 mature (≥ 0) and 26 immature (< 0) structures (Fig.  3 B), and visual overlays of TLS maturation showed near-perfect concordance with histology (Fig.  3 C). Area-normalized transcriptional profiling of the 13 chemokines and their receptors revealed a sharp dichotomy (Fig.  3 D): mature TLSs contained significantly more  CXCL13  and  CXCR4 , whereas immature TLSs were enriched for  CCL2 ,  CCL3 ,  CCL4 ,  CCL5 ,  CCL8 ,  CCL18  and the IFN-inducible  CXCL9–11  cluster. TLS-area–adjusted cell counts mirrored these findings, with higher densities of every B-cell subset in mature TLSs, and predominantly CD8⁺ T cells, macrophages, mDCs and endothelial cells in their immature counterparts (Fig.  3 E). ( H ) Kaplan–Meier overall survival for immunotherapy-treated patients ( n  = 45) stratified by mature TLS (red) versus immature or absent TLS (blue)                   Single-cell analysis clarified delineated distinct molecular programs associated with TLS maturation. In mature TLSs, fibroblasts showed higher  CXCL12 , whereas FoBs exhibited elevated  CXCR4  [ 36 ]. Tfh cells expressed abundant  CXCL13  together with  CXCR5  on B cells [ 33 ]. In contrast, immature TLSs exhibited a Th1-skewed inflammatory milieu characterized by  CXCL9  from IFN-γ-responsive macrophages and DCs, and higher  IFIT3  in CD8⁺ T cells. Endothelial transcriptomics reinforced this functional divergence: mature TLS vasculature preferentially expressed PNAd-associated genes, such as  CHST4  and  B3GNT3  together with adhesion molecules, including  SELP  and  ICAM1 , whereas immature TLSs overexpressed the HEV-developmental receptors  LTBR  and  TNFRSF14  (Fig.  3 F and Supplementary Fig. S6). Gene Ontology analysis echoed these contrasts, identifying enrichment of adaptive B-cell programs in mature TLSs and pathways governing lymphocyte migration, cell–cell adhesion, and activation thresholds in immature TLSs (Fig.  3 G).  Kaplan–Meier curves in immunotherapy-treated patients demonstrated that mature TLSs conferred a substantial survival advantage over immature or absent TLSs (median OS 60.2 vs. 21.4 months; log-rank  P  = 0.037) (Fig.  3 H). Collectively, these spatial and transcriptional features characterize TLS maturation states and demonstrate their prognostic relevance in patients receiving immunotherapy.    ID1-high HEVs in mature TLS are associated with better survival in patients receiving immunotherapy  Unsupervised UMAP analysis of the pre-processed, normalized endothelial subset resolved two transcriptionally discrete vascular clusters: high endothelial cell (HEC) and blood endothelial cell (BEC) (Fig.  4 A and Supplementary Fig. S7). The HEC cluster was characterized by robust expression of classical HEV genes, including  ACKR1 ,  SELP ,  LTBR  and  TNFRSF14 , confirming its HEV-like phenotype (Fig.  4 B) [ 30 ]. MIF of resected samples corroborated the spatial coexistence of both HEC- and BEC-type vessels within mature TLSs in situ (Fig.  4 C). Differential-expression analysis of HECs revealed significant upregulation of  ID1  in mature TLSs compared with immature TLSs (Fig.  4 D,  P  < 0.05). Compared with the other ID family members,  ID2  and  ID4 ,  ID1  was selectively expressed in endothelial cells, with the highest levels observed in HECs (Fig.  4 E, F). We further re-analyzed an integrated scRNA-seq dataset comprising 185 NSCLC samples to validate ID-family expression in the vascular compartment [ 19 ].  ID1  expression was largely confined to malignant epithelial and endothelial cells. Within the endothelial lineage, its expression was observed across several subpopulations, including mature HECs. In mature HECs,  ID1  was frequently expressed, whereas  ID2  and  ID4  were rarely detected (Supplementary Fig. S8). These findings are broadly consistent with our spatial transcriptomic analysis.    Fig. 4   Endothelial-focused spatial transcriptomic and MIF analyses within TLSs. MIF consistently showed strong ID1 protein staining in the HECs of mature TLSs, although some HECs lacked ID1 staining (Fig.  4 I). Functionally, the adhesion signature for HECs, calculated from PNAd-associated genes, together with  SELE ,  SELP ,  ICAM1 , and  VCAM1 , was significantly higher in mature TLSs than in immature TLSs (Fig.  4 J,  P  < 0.05). Consistent with this, mature TLSs showed markedly higher normalized numbers of conventional B, CD4 + T, and CD8⁺ T cells residing within 100 μm of a HEC (Fig.  4 K,  P  < 0.05).  In the biomarker validation cohort ( n  = 45), 18 patients (40%) had ID1-high HEVs, whereas the remaining 27 patients (60%) had ID1-low HEVs or lacked mature TLSs (baseline characteristics are summarized in Supplementary Table S3). Patients with tumors with ID1-high HEVs showed a markedly higher objective response rate (61%) compared with those with ID1-low HEVs (17%) or without mature TLSs (7%) (Fig.  4 L,  P  < 0.05). Likewise, Kaplan–Meier analysis showed a pronounced survival advantage among patients with ID1-high HEVs, with median OS not reached versus 21.4 months in the ID1-low HEVs/absent mature TLSs groups (Fig.  4 M, log-rank  P  < 0.001). Furthermore, multivariate analysis identified the presence of ID1-high HEVs as an independent prognostic factor (Table  2 ). Finally, responders and non-responders showed no clear differences in baseline characteristics within the ID1-high group, suggesting the limits of ID1-high HEVs as a predictor (Supplementary Table S4). Together, these data identify ID1-high HEVs as a functional hallmark of mature TLSs and a robust biomarker of enhanced immunotherapy efficacy and survival in NSCLC. TLS-area–normalized cell counts confirmed treatment-specific re-patterning, with increased conventional and follicular B cell densities under ICB therapy, whereas central-proliferating B cells were unchanged and exhibited lower  MKI67  expression. CXCR4  levels also increased consistently across these cell types (Fig.  5 D, E). Furthermore, spatial CCI maps demonstrated that TLSs in ICB–treated tumors displayed stronger  CXCL12–CXCR4  signaling than those in untreated controls (Fig.  5 F). Within this pathway, fibroblasts showed the strongest communication probabilities with follicular B cells (Fig.  5 G). Nearest-neighbor distances between fibroblasts and FoBs were comparable in the control and ICB cohort (Fig.  5 H). Among the fibroblast subsets, PDGFRA⁺ fibroblasts were identified as the population most likely to interact with FoBs through the CXCL12–CXCR4 axis (Supplementary Fig. S9) [ 37 ]. High  CXCL12  expression within TLSs has been proposed to correlate with greater immune-cell infiltration and favor antitumor activity [ 38 ]. Consistent with this notion, patients with NSCLC treated with immunotherapy for tumors harboring CXCL12-high TLSs showed a significantly longer OS compared with those with CXCL12-low or TLS-negative tumors (median OS 60.2 vs. 26.6 months; log-rank  P  = 0.014) (Fig.  5 I, J). In summary, immunotherapy-driven tumor regression enhanced  CXCL12–CXCR4  signaling, suggesting that patients with TLSs bearing this  CXCL12 -high niche may have a greater survival benefit from ICB therapy. ICB–treated tumors contained fewer PNAd-positive HEV per square millimeter than control, indicating a treatment-related reduction in HEV density (Fig.  6 A, B). TLS-associated HECs from ICB–treated tumors exhibited a transcriptional shift in which adhesion genes including  SELE  and  SELP  together with the PNAd-biosynthetic module — B3GNT3 ,  CHST4 ,  FUT7 ,  GCNT1  and  ST3GAL4 — were likewise suppressed, and the differentiation brake  ID1  fell sharply, along with  ID2  (Fig.  6 C, D). In contrast, angio-remodeling transcripts, including  ANGPT1 ,  ANGPT2 ,  VEGFA ,  APLN ,  APLNR , and  FLT1 , increased. However, VEGFA expression within endothelial cells was minimal, and the ligand was predominantly supplied by fibroblasts rather than by HEVs themselves (Supplementary Fig. 10). Gene Ontology analysis consistently shows that ICB therapy redirected HECs from an immune-recruitment program toward vascular remodeling: genes that are upregulated in the treated group clustered within angiogenesis pathways, whereas those enriched in controls were related to immune trafficking (Fig.  6 E). Furthermore, ICB therapy significantly decreased an adhesion signature per TLS, defined by  B3GNT3 ,  CHST4 ,  FUT7 ,  GCNT1 ,  ST3GAL4 ,  SELE ,  SELP ,  ICAM1  and  VCAM1 , while simultaneously amplifying an angio-remodel signature comprising  ANGPT1 ,  ANGPT2 ,  APLN ,  APLNR ,  FLT1  and  TEK  (Fig.  6 F, G). Functionally, the normalized counts of conventional B, CD4⁺ T, and CD8⁺ T cells located within 100 μm of a HEC were significantly reduced in the ICB cohort (Fig.  6 H,  P  < 0.05). Finally, MIF showed markedly reduced ID1 protein in TLS-associated HECs from ICB–treated tumors compared with controls, mirroring the transcriptomic downregulation described above (Fig.  6 I, J). In summary, TLS-associated HEVs potentially shift phenotypically with TLS maturation and treatment. In immature TLS, HEVs first express the LTβR axis and homing chemokines, recruiting lymphocytes via nascent HEC cuffs with BECs. During maturation,  ID1  increases, and classical adhesion features together with the PNAd-synthetic enzyme set predominates, yielding a fully functional “mature HEV.” ICB ultimately regresses tumors and drives the vessels into a remodeled endothelial state: ID1 levels fall sharply, the adhesion/PNAd module contracts, and lymphocyte influx diminishes, while vascular-remodeling genes are induced, preserving structural plasticity (Fig.  6 K). In the present study, we aimed to map how TLS composition and endothelial dynamics varied with maturation and treatment, and link these mechanistic insights to clinical outcomes to elucidate their contribution to TLS-mediated antitumor immunity.  This study provides an integrated spatial-omics framework unifying the cellular and clinical dimensions of TLSs in NSCLC, particularly in endothelial populations. By combining high-sensitivity in situ transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence, and immunotherapy-related clinical outcomes, we delineate three key principles: (i) TLS maturation establishes novel immune niches in NSCLC, (ii) ID1-high HEVs within mature TLSs confer clinical benefit, and (iii) ICB therapy reprograms HEVs from a lymphocyte-recruiting phenotype to a vascular-reprogramming state while enhancing a  CXCL12-CXCR4  niche.  Spatial transcriptomics is indispensable for analyzing TLS biology. TLSs juxtapose lymphoid, myeloid, and stromal elements in complex three-dimensional assemblies. Therefore, only methods that preserve tissue coordinates and resolve individual cells can reveal their true organization. The Xenium In Situ platforms provide sub-micrometer, in-situ detection of transcripts, enabling the visual validation of cell annotations and tracking of follicles, vessels, and related microstructure continuity throughout an entire TLS. By applying this platform, we profiled > 300,000 TLS-resident cells at single-cell resolution to obtain a nearly exhaustive annotation of every anatomical component. We further expanded the standard immuno-oncology panel with vascular-specific genes, allowing cytokine and chemokine quantification across all cell types, with a focus on endothelial cells.  Consistent with our observations, studies in both hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric cancer show that mature TLSs are characterized by  CXCL13 -rich, B-cell-dominated cores, whereas immature aggregates show enrichment of  CXCL9-11  and Th1-skewed signatures [ 23 ,  39 ]. While single-cell studies on HEVs in human tumors are limited, analogous analyses in human lymph nodes are increasing [ 30 ,  40 ]. These nodal datasets have demonstrated that PNAd-positive HEVs form a discrete endothelial cluster characterized by high expression of adhesion genes such as  SELE ,  SELP ,  B3GNT3  and  CHST4 , whereas BECs segregate as a separate population lacking immune-trafficking functions. These observations are consistent with our findings, supporting the conclusion that TLS maturation is conserved across different organs and tumor types.  ID1 is a basic helix-loop-helix transcriptional regulator lacking a DNA-binding motif. Instead, it heterodimerizes with canonical bHLH factors, blocking lineage-specific transcription and sustaining a proliferative, undifferentiated state. Its expression is induced by a variety of upstream cues, including BMP/SMAD1-5, TGF-β, VEGF-A/VEGFR2, hypoxia-stabilized HIF-1α, Wnt/β-catenin, and inflammatory cytokines [ 41 ]. In tumors,  ID1  is enriched mainly in malignant and endothelial cells and promotes metastasis and angiogenesis; therefore, its overexpression correlates with poor prognosis. However, its involvement in HEVs remains unreported [ 42 ]. Lyden et al. showed that physiological  ID  expression is indispensable for angiogenesis in  ID  knockout mouse models, in which endothelial cells lacking  ID1  emerged in tumor xenografts but did not lumenize or generate properly branched vessels [ 43 ]. Accordingly, ID family genes are critical for synchronizing endothelial differentiation with the invasive expansion of the vascular network. Typically, high  ID1  expression in bulk lung tumor tissue is linked to poor prognosis, whereas our data show that within TLSs, elevated  ID1  levels trend toward improved clinical outcomes [ 44 ]. Such  ID1 -like “context-dependent inversions” are likewise observed for several other genes within the TLS compartment. Although the  CXCL12–CXCR4  axis is classically pro-tumorigenic outside TLSs, promoting metastasis, angiogenesis, and immune evasion through ERK1/2, Ras, p38 MAPK, PLC/MAPK, and JNK cascades [ 45 ], CXCL12 expression in combined hepatocellular–cholangiocarcinoma correlates positively with TLS density, TLS maturation, and favorable prognosis, suggesting that within TLSs this axis may instead support lymphoid organization and maturation [ 38 ]. In parallel, a recent study in hepatocellular carcinoma demonstrated that chemotherapy-induced TLS formation is likewise driven by CXCL12–CXCR4–mediated recruitment of immune and stromal cells, further reinforcing the notion that this axis can acquire a TLS-promoting role in specific therapeutic contexts [ 46 ]. Collectively, these observations highlight that signaling pathways traditionally viewed as oncogenic can adopt distinct, TLS-restricted functions, underscoring the need to dissect TLS-specific vascular pathways when developing HEV-focused immuno-oncology strategies.  CXCL13 is a recognized marker of follicular TLS cores and favorable outcome [ 14 ,  47 ]. In our data, the CXCL13 load per TLS was comparable between the control and ICB-treated cohorts, whereas CXCR5 expression was increased in ICB-treated TLSs. This dissociation suggests that ICB does not globally amplify CXCL13 production itself, but rather selectively enhances the responsiveness of B cells and Tfh to a relatively stable CXCL13 field. By contrast, knowledge regarding chemokines other than CXCL13 remains limited. Our data show that ICB selectively augments  CXCL12  expression in fibroblasts. Although the mechanistic link between PD-1 signaling and  CXCL12  induction remains to be elucidated, the increase in CXCL12 parallels a modest association between PD-L1 TPS and TLS maturation [ 13 ]. Consistent with independent spatial omics studies, mature TLSs displayed strikingly high  CXCL12  levels, mirroring the  CXCL13  pattern, suggesting that, in this compartmentalized niche,  CXCL12  may emerge as a biomarker of durable benefits in immunotherapy-treated patients rather than a canonical pro-tumorigenic signal [ 38 ]. Nevertheless, multivariate models incorporating TLS maturation as a confounder did not identify CXCL12 as an independent predictor, underscoring the need for cautious interpretation. In contrast, ID1 retained its independent prognostic significance even after adjustment, despite possible unmeasured immunosuppressive factors limiting its predictive value. Although our study is retrospective and does not allow longitudinal tracking of individual HEVs, one possible interpretation is that an ID1-high, functionally active HEV niche is well established at baseline in tumors that ultimately respond to ICB. In contrast, such an ID1-high niche may be insufficiently formed or inadequately maintained in non-responders. These post-treatment changes do not contradict the prognostic relevance of baseline ID1-high HEVs. Baseline ID1-high HEVs in untreated tumors reflect a reactive, lymphocyte-recruiting program that facilitates antitumor immunity and predicts ICI benefit, similar to reports showing that pre-existing HEV-rich tumors are associated with improved clinical outcomes [ 48 ]. In contrast, the ID1-low, PNAd-low, angiogenic-signature–high state observed after ICI likely represents a physiological reprogramming process during the resolution of inflammation, in which HEVs transition from a recruitment-competent phenotype to a vascular-maintenance or retention-type state. Thus, the baseline predictive role of ID1 and its post-therapy reduction correspond to distinct temporal phases of HEV biology rather than opposing biological effects. In summary, our work illustrates ID1 as a novel predictive and monitoring biomarker, although its regulatory mechanisms require further research.  The principal strength of this study was the application of Xenium In Situ, which preserved the native continuity of TLSs and their vasculature while providing single-cell resolution. Conventional scRNA-seq–derived “TLS-mimic” datasets cannot attain this fidelity: our approach profiled > 300,000 TLS-resident cells and retained intact follicles and vessels, which allowed the direct assessment of CCIs and HEV-mediated lymphocyte recruitment. We then validated the markers identified through this spatial screening in independent immunotherapy cohorts, thereby establishing ID1 as a clinically relevant biomarker associated with survival. However, the study has several limitations. First, the target-gene panel was relatively small. Although the default set captures core cell-type markers, it does not include essential TLS genes such as  BCL6  and  AICDA , which should be custom-added for deeper analyses. Second, the discovery and validation cohorts were modest in size and retrospective in design; thus, selection bias was possible, and the generalizability of the findings is limited. To address these issues, a prospective study with a larger patient cohort is warranted.  In conclusion, our data revealed a link between TLS maturation or ICB therapy and HEC differentiation, in which  ID1  plays a pivotal regulatory role. In mature TLSs, HECs display high  ID1  expression, actively recruit lymphocytes, and are associated with favorable clinical outcomes. However, after ICB induced tumor regressions,  ID1  and adhesion transcripts in HECs decreased sharply, lymphocyte ingress wanes, and a vascular remodeling-signature was induced. Therefore, ID1 has emerged as a dynamic biomarker in patients treated with immunotherapy. Collectively, these findings provide a mechanistic framework and a practical biomarker set for HEV-focused immuno-oncology strategies.    Supplementary Information

evidence_text:
Single-Cell Lineage Trajectory Defines Cyclin-Dependent Kinase Inhibitor-Sensitive Cells-of-Origin in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

Background and aims

Understanding the cells of origin is essential for overcoming therapy resistance and improving early intervention strategies in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). Despite recent advances in genomic profiling, the precise cellular hierarchies and molecular programs driving ESCC initiation remain poorly defined.

Methods

We utilized machine learning-based single-cell trajectory analysis on 4-nitroquinoline 1-oxide-induced murine models and genetically engineered organoids to identify cellular lineages during tumorigenesis. Combined with gene regulatory network analysis, we identified transcriptional drivers of tumor initiation and employed transcriptome-based drug repurposing to predict compounds targeting these initiating populations.

Results

Our analyses revealed multiple distinct epithelial clusters that function as cellular origins of ESCC, exhibiting diverse stem and progenitor signatures. Gene regulatory network analysis of these populations indicated activation of stem/progenitor cell regulators, including CEBPβ and TFAP2A/C. Translating these findings, a transcriptome-based drug repurposing screen identified 5 chemical candidates, 4 of which are potent cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, aligning with the frequent loss-of-function mutations in TP53 and CDKN2A observed in ESCC. Notably, CDK inhibitors markedly inhibit ESCC cell proliferation.

Conclusion

This research delineates the potential cellular origins of ESCC and their key regulons, thereby pioneering a single-cell-derived therapeutic strategy that exposes vulnerabilities in tumor-initiating cells.

evidence_text:
High-definition spatial transcriptomic profiling of immune cell populations in colorectal cancer. A comprehensive understanding of cellular behavior and response to the tumor microenvironment (TME) in colorectal cancer (CRC) remains elusive. Here, we introduce the high-definition Visium spatial transcriptomic technology (Visium HD) and investigate formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded human CRC samples (n = 5). We demonstrate the high sensitivity, single-cell-scale resolution and spatial accuracy of Visium HD, generating a highly refined whole-transcriptome spatial profile of CRC samples. We identify transcriptomically distinct macrophage subpopulations in different spatial niches with potential pro-tumor and anti-tumor functions via interactions with tumor and T cells. In situ gene expression analysis validates our findings and localizes a clonally expanded T cell population close to macrophages with anti-tumor features. Our study demonstrates the power of high-resolution spatial technologies to understand cellular interactions in the TME and paves the way for larger studies that will unravel mechanisms and biomarkers of CRC biology, improving diagnosis and disease management strategies. Main  CRC accounted for 9.4% of cancer-related deaths (0.9 million) in 2020, and its global incidence is predicted to double by 2035 (refs.   1 , 2  ). Its poor 5-year survival rate highlights the need for better early detection and prognostic biomarkers for future disease management  3  . Growing evidence suggests that tumor heterogeneity is best described at the transcriptome level, rather than with classical histopathological or mutation-centered disease classifications  4  . Technologies that refine our understanding of the TME, including the diverse roles of innate and adaptive immune responses and cellular crosstalk in CRC, have the potential to inform better clinical intervention strategies.  Sequencing-based genomic technologies have played an important role in building our knowledge of CRC biology  4 – 7  . However, bulk sequencing, which involves averages data from cells and tissues, is confounded by the complexities of the TME and intratumor heterogeneity. Single-cell transcriptomic (single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq)) technologies have partially filled this gap and allowed for detailed exploration of the cell types within the TME in CRC  8 – 16  . Although these studies add critical single-cell-level resolution to our understanding of CRC, they lack any information about the cellular organization within the tissue. Spatial transcriptomics offers a solution. Several commercial technologies are currently available, including Visium CytAssist Spatial Gene Expression (‘Visium v2’, 10x Genomics), STOmics (BGI) and Curio Seeker (Curio Bioscience). Other published methods include Seq-Scope  17  , Nova-ST  18  , Open-ST  19  , HDST  20  , DBiT-seq  21  , Pixel-seq  22   and XYZeq  23  . These methods have enabled the localization of cell types within tissues, which is critical for understanding the interaction between cells in the TME of CRC  24 – 27  . However, these technologies lack resolution at the single-cell scale or are typically only compatible with freshly frozen tissues, and, as such, a deep understanding of tumor organization based on readily available biobanked samples remains elusive.  Here, we introduce Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression (‘Visium HD’), a whole-transcriptome assay with single-cell-scale resolution compatible with freshly frozen, fixed frozen and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) samples. The Visium HD slides provide a dramatically increased oligonucleotide barcode density (~11,000,000 continuous 2-µm features in a 6.5 × 6.5-mm Visium HD capture area, compared to ~5,000 55-µm features with gaps between the equivalent Visium v2 capture area), generating data that can be binned in square features. We demonstrate the use of Visium HD as a discovery platform by profiling CRC FFPE tissue blocks from multiple patients. The single-cell-scale resolution of Visium HD allowed us to map distinct populations of immune cells, specifically macrophages and T cells, and evaluate DGE at the tumor boundary. We also generated a multi-patient single-cell reference dataset from a larger cohort of FFPE samples and used it to annotate deconvolved Visium HD data bins, validating the cell type populations identified by Visium HD and subsequently using the integrated data to comprehensively map the cellular composition and molecular signatures of the TME in CRC. Leveraging the high resolution of Visium HD, we examined the cells at the immediate periphery (within 50 µm) of the tumor. This allowed us to spatially map distinct macrophage subpopulations to specific tumor regions, to compare their transcriptomic profiles, which indicate that they may exert pro-tumor roles via different pathways, and to characterize cell–cell interactions. To validate the spatial accuracy of Visium HD, we analyzed a subset of genes using an independent spatial technology (Xenium In Situ Gene Expression  28  ). We confirmed the presence of the two pro-tumor macrophage subpopulations in different tumor niches and pinpointed the location of the T cells within the TME. We also detected a clonally expanded T cell population and the microenvironment in which it resides, revealing a macrophage-containing niche with anti-tumor features.  Our study underscores the importance of using high-resolution spatial technologies in exploring the heterogeneity of cancer biology. These advanced tools are crucial for precisely mapping diverse immune cell niches and elucidating the complex interactions between these cells and their microenvironment. Spatial technologies provide a detailed understanding of spatial variations in cell types, their subpopulations and cell-to-cell relationships, which are key to developing targeted therapies and personalized treatment approaches. The combination of whole-transcriptome and targeted in situ spatial technologies used in our investigation provides a deep insight into the complex and dynamic nature of the TME, highlighting the importance of spatial context in understanding cancer heterogeneity and disease progression.    Results  Visium HD enables transcriptome-wide spatial gene expression analysis at single-cell scale. Gene expression is measured by the capture of ligated probe pairs targeting the whole protein-coding transcriptome. We profiled tumor biopsies from five patients with colorectal adenocarcinoma, in addition to normal adjacent tissue (NAT) from three of these patients (Table  1 ). Serial sections of FFPE tissues were used to benchmark the technology performance or to explore the TME using Visium HD. Additionally, selected serial sections were used to generate an scRNA-seq dataset and for in situ gene expression analysis (Fig.  1 ). Sections from the same FFPE blocks were assayed with scRNA-seq (Chromium Single Cell Gene Expression Flex;  n  = 8). Technology performance comparisons were made using data from matched datasets.                    Visium HD specifications and performance  The Visium HD capture array consists of 2 × 2-µm squares of uniquely barcoded oligonucleotides directly adjacent to each other on the slide, resulting in a continuous lawn of capture oligonucleotides. This represents an increase of several orders of magnitude in barcode complexity over earlier Visium slides, which have 55-µm circular capture areas with a 100-µm center to center gaps between them (Fig.  2a,b ). For downstream analysis, the Space Ranger (version 3.0) pipeline outputs the raw 2-µm data and data binned at 8- and 16-µm resolution. Unless otherwise described, we used the 8-µm binned data in our analyses. Source data                    To assess Visium HD performance, we analyzed serial sections from a normal colon mucosa sample run on Visium v2 and Visium HD. Visium HD generated notably higher-resolution data, as shown by the improved unsupervised clustering, both in terms of the refined specificity of the clusters and the ability to map them to morphological features of the colon mucosal tissue (Fig.  2c ). Whole-transcriptome unique molecular identifier (UMI) counts at similar sequencing depth showed a strong correlation between the two technologies (Fig.  2d ,  R  2  = 0.82 and Extended Data Fig.  1 ,  R  2  = 0.81 and 0.90), indicating that the Visium HD assay maintains the high assay sensitivity of Visium v2 (Supplementary Table  1 ).                    The estimated fraction of molecules arising from off-target probe binding events, that is, probes binding to genomic DNA (gDNA), was reduced in Visium HD (average of 4.13% in Visium v2 and 0.70% in Visium HD) (Supplementary Table  1 ). To assess any potential bias arising from such events, these probes were computationally excluded for this analysis, after which we observed a stronger correlation between the UMI counts from the different assays ( R  2  = 0.92, Fig.  2d ;  R  2  = 0.93 and 0.96, Extended Data Fig.  1 ).  In array-based spatial technologies, the analyte to be measured (messenger RNA (mRNA) itself or a ligated probe reporting on the mRNA) must move from the tissue to come in contact with the array. Precise transfer of analytes with minimal lateral movement is essential to ensure that the spatial transcript measurements are representative of the biology of the tissue being analyzed. To achieve this, tissue placement and subsequent molecular biology reactions must be carefully controlled to minimize lateral movement of transcripts or their proxies away from the site of origin. Similar to the Visium v2 assay, Visium HD uses the CytAssist instrument. The CytAssist controls reagent flow and thus allows target molecules from the tissue to be captured upon release, preventing free diffusion of transcripts and ensuring accurate transfer of analytes from tissues to the capture arrays. The spatial fidelity gains afforded by the CytAssist have been described previously  29 , 30   (technical note  CG000618 , revision B). To quantify the spatial accuracy of Visium HD, we analyzed genes with distinct localization to the glands of normal colon mucosal tissue (goblet cell gene markers:  CLCA1 ,  FCGBP  and  MUC2 ). In each tissue section, we manually selected four regions of interest (ROIs) and, for each marker gene, quantified the number of UMIs that were within or outside of the annotated structures in which their expression is expected based on established expression patterns  31  . We observed that most transcripts (98.3–99%) were localized in their expected morphological locations within the source masks, and only a small proportion (0.97–1.73%) were in adjacent masks (Fig.  2e  and Extended Data Fig.  2 ), consistent with faithful transfer of ligated probes from the tissue to the array at single-cell-scale resolution. An initial analysis of the combined dataset identified 23 clusters grouped into nine major cell types (tumor, intestinal epithelial, endothelial, smooth muscle, T cells, fibroblasts, B cells, myeloid, neuronal) and one unknown cluster (a cell cluster with a gene expression profile that did not readily match any known cell type), which aligned with the expected morphological features of the tissues (Fig.  3a ). As an orthogonal measurement of cells present in normal and diseased colon samples, we generated a single-cell reference atlas of 260,506 cells from serial FFPE sections of normal and CRC tissues ( n  = 8; Table  1 ). We used this dataset as a reference to deconvolve the HD data, which yielded a highly resolved map of the cell types within the tissue resembling the expected tissue morphology (Fig.  3b ). Each patient sample was associated with a major and distinct tumor cell type (Extended Data Figs.  4  and  5 ) that mapped onto the tumor regions across each tissue section. We validated the spatial arrangement of these cell labels in Visium HD with the expression of well-known markers such as  PIGR  (goblet cells and enterocytes) , CEACAM6  (tumor) and  COL1A1  (fibroblasts) (Fig.  3c ). When we compared the unsupervised clustering to the deconvolution results, we found that cell types with stereotypical morphological organization (for example, goblet cells and enterocytes in colon glands) can be identified based on the Visium HD clustering data alone. However, deconvolution based on single-cell data was useful for identifying subtypes of cells with a more random organization or very small cells, for example, B cell and T cell subtypes (Extended Data Fig.  6 ). We used a custom distance-based analysis to identify all barcoded 8-µm bins within 50 µm of the regions we had labeled as tumor cells via spot deconvolution (Fig.  4a ). We reasoned that a 50-µm radius around tumor cells was likely to contain cells that are either directly interacting with the tumor cells or influencing the TME. We quantified the cellular composition of these regions compared to those identified in the rest of the tissue. In all tissue blocks, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) were the most prominent cell type while macrophages were consistently identified as the most abundant immune cell type (Fig.  4b ) in regions proximal to tumor cells. We corroborated these findings by examining the expression of known macrophage ( C1QC ) and CAF ( COL1A1 ) markers (Fig.  4a ). We identified two macrophage subpopulations with specific gene expression profiles mainly defined by expression of  SELENOP  or  SPP1  genes (Fig.  4c ). Density estimation analysis revealed that the highly enriched regions of these macrophage subpopulations in the TME were mostly in distinct spatial niches (Fig.  4d ). We observed that  SELENOP+  macrophages were enriched for pathways involved in processes such as inflammatory response, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) signaling via NF-κB, apoptosis, and response to ultraviolet radiation. Meanwhile,  SPP1+  macrophages were enriched for genes involved in coagulation, cholesterol homeostasis and upregulation of KRAS signaling pathways. Notably, the epithelial–mesenchymal transition pathway and complement system were upregulated in both macrophage subpopulations (Fig.  5a ). Analysis of the tumor cells revealed that the different macrophage subpopulations were localized in tumor regions that also had distinct gene expression profiles. Tumor cells in areas enriched for  SPP1+  macrophages showed differential expression of  TGFBI  and  PERP  genes (Fig.  5b ), while tumor regions closer to  SELENOP+  macrophages were enriched for  REG1A  and  REG1B  genes (patient P1CRC) or the  LCN2  gene (P2CRC and P5CRC; Fig.  5b ). While  REG1A  and  REG1B  enrichment near  SELENOP+  macrophages was primarily observed in P1CRC, we found upregulated expression of these genes in P2CRC goblet cells within the  SELENOP+  macrophage niche. To better understand the T cell response, we explored the clonality of the antigen recognizing T cell receptors (TCRs) of the T cells in and around the CRC tumors. Using T cells isolated from dissociated tumor cells from the same patients, we performed Single Cell Immune Profiling to obtain the TCR sequences. This revealed a clonotype with 11% representation within the T cell population of sample P5CRC (TRAV38-1–TRAJ58; TRAB38-2/DV8–TRAJ57; TRBV4-2–TRBJ2-1; Supplementary Table  4 ) but no expansions in the other samples. No complementarity-determining region 3 (CDR3) matches to this clonotype were found in VDJdb ( https://vdjdb.cdr3.net/ ), indicating that this clonotype recognizes a neoepitope specific to this tumor.  As expanded clonotypes indicate an active adaptive immune response, we sought to localize these cells within the tissue. We designed probes targeting the CDR3 regions of the expanded clonotype and included them in the Xenium custom add-on panel (Supplementary Table  3 ). Xenium analysis identified clusters of clonally expanded CD8 +  T cells residing close to tumor cells and within gut-associated lymphoid tissues (Fig.  7g,h ). These T cells were localized within  CXCL9 -,  CXCL10 - and  CXCL11 -expressing foci, where  STAB1+  macrophages, B cells and endothelial cells were present and contributing to the expression of these chemokines (Fig.  7h ), known to recruit immune cells to the tumor site  37  . This observation was validated in the corresponding region of the Visium HD data (Fig.  7i ).  TRAC+  T cells were identified near  CEACAM5+  tumor cells,  SELENOP+  C1QC+  macrophages and  JCHAIN  B cells.  SELENOP  and  JCHAIN  were not included in the Xenium gene panel but were included in our analysis based on the Visium HD data, highlighting the complementary strengths of Xenium and Visium HD technologies.     Discussion  The advent of spatial transcriptomics has enabled a more comprehensive understanding of biology in health and disease and is particularly relevant in oncology, where the localization of specific cell types in the TME can have prognostic implications. By enabling precise mapping of the TME, these technologies reveal the complex spatial relationships among cells, which are crucial for understanding tumor progression and resistance to therapy. However, existing technologies have limitations related to resolution, tissue compatibility or ease of use. In this study, we introduced Visium HD, the next generation of the Visium technology, and used it to explore the TME in FFPE colon adenocarcinoma samples. We first demonstrated the high sensitivity, resolution and accuracy of Visium HD. Taking advantage of these features, we explored the immune cell composition in the immediate vicinity of CRC tumors, their potential role and interplay with other immune and tumor cells.  Immune cell interactions in the CRC TME remain poorly understood, with TAMs showing controversial roles due to mixed M1–M2 polarization and spatial distribution  26  . For example, it has been hypothesized that tumor cells at the invasive front affect macrophage polarization  26  . Visium HD enabled whole-transcriptome analysis within the spatially complex tumor boundary niche, with micrometer-level precision across a large tissue section, which has not been possible with existing technologies. We discovered macrophage populations with distinct gene expression profiles, unique spatial distributions and specific enriched pathways from data obtained from single archived tissue sections from different patients. Both  SPP1+  and  SELENOP+  macrophages are enriched in tumor tissues and more likely to adopt an M2-like phenotype exerting pro-tumor and pro-metastatic roles  9 , 26 , 38 , 39  . In our samples, the spatial distribution of both macrophage subtypes and the upregulation of genes in known tumorigenic pathways  40   further support a pro-tumor role in the TME.  SPP1+  macrophages were adjacent to tumor cells expressing  TGFBI  and  PERP , and  SELENOP+  macrophages were adjacent to tumor cells expressing  REG1A  and  LCN2  genes, all genes that have been associated with metastasis, advanced tumor stage and poor prognosis  41 – 44  . Moreover, the predicted ligand–receptor communication between  SPP1+  (via SPP1–CD44) and  SELENOP+  (via B2M–KLRD1) macrophages with CD8 +  T cells in the TME could ultimately lead to reduced immune surveillance and evasion of the immune system by inhibiting cytotoxic activity  45 – 47  . These data suggest different pro-tumor mechanisms exerted by macrophage populations in different TME niches.  While  REG1A  expression initially seemed exclusive to a particular set of tumor cells, a granular subclustering analysis of goblet cells revealed a distinct subpopulation expressing  REG1A , with features of both goblet cells and  REG1A+  tumor cells. While these  REG1A+  cells exhibited reduced DGE of goblet cell markers, they exhibited higher DGE of  REG1A  tumor-associated features. These  REG1A  +  goblet cells likely represent a transitional state of tumorigenesis, as  REG1A  may be involved in early tumor development in CRC  48  . Without Visium HD, identification and localization of this transitional goblet population would have been challenging.  The pro-tumor features displayed by macrophage subpopulations and the potential role in inhibiting immune cell proliferation and function led us to further our analysis on the T cells near the tumors. T cell infiltration into CRC tumors has been associated with favorable outcomes, suggesting a possible role for immunoediting in controlling tumor growth  35  . Using Xenium, we mapped the location of clonally expanded T cells within the CRC TME at single-cell resolution. These clonally expanded T cells colocalized with cells expressing  CXCL9 ,  CXCL10  and  CXCL11 , encoding chemokines, which are known to attract cytotoxic T lymphocytes  37  . Consistent with this finding, these expanded T cells expressed cytotoxic genes, including  PRF1 ,  GZMA  and  GZMK . Notably, macrophages within these regions emerged as the primary source of  CXCL9 ,  CXCL10  and  CXCL11  expression. This finding suggests that, despite the overall immunosuppressive TME, there are niches of anti-tumor immune responses where T cells are actively recruited to the tumor boundary. This is an important observation, as the balance between the pro-tumor and anti-tumor macrophages influences tumor progression and therapy response. Further research into macrophage plasticity and their ability to switch between these states could provide potential targets for cancer management strategies  49 , 50  . Identifying key biomarkers that signify this transition enables the development of new therapeutic targets, which have the potential to allow for earlier-stage, targeted and personalized cancer treatments. A limitation of this study is the small sample size, preventing us from drawing broad conclusions. However, we demonstrate that high-resolution spatial technologies can provide comprehensive insights that will be key in identifying biomarkers as potential therapeutic targets for CRC. This study lays the groundwork for future breakthroughs using larger cohorts.  Future studies using more sophisticated analyses can take full advantage of the 2-µm data afforded by Visium HD. While our nuclear segmentation analysis using the 2-µm resolution data allowed us to locate T cells within the tumor boundaries, truly accurate cell type assignment requires advanced cell segmentation algorithms that are not yet available. This could be accomplished by either using cell surface staining information or through the development of spatially aware methods capable of including information from neighboring bins during unsupervised clustering  51  . These methods would also account for small cells and cells in dense neighborhoods, mitigating any need for a single-cell reference dataset.  High-definition spatial technologies are providing increasingly detailed information into cancer biology. Our results exemplify the valuable insights gained from studying immune cell populations in the TME with high-definition, whole-transcriptome spatial technologies and pave the way for future research to improve our understanding of tumor evolution and to inform therapeutic advances. Our study combined whole-transcriptome and targeted in situ spatial technologies to obtain additional information on the TME heterogenic nature. Given the poor survival rates of many cancers, there is a pressing need for better diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers to inform clinical strategies.  Leveraging high-definition spatial technologies on large cohort studies to characterize cells in tumors, in combination with cutting-edge analytical approaches powered by machine learning and artificial intelligence, will yield a detailed appreciation of tumor heterogeneity and the cell-to-cell interactions in these different TME niches and the identification of spatially resolved biomarkers. This understanding will provide critical insights into tumor evolution and treatment resistance, guiding the identification of crucial biomarkers and the development of targeted therapies.    Methods   Biomaterials  Human biological samples were obtained from Discovery Life Sciences. The research use of these specimens was approved by the corresponding institutional review boards under protocol numbers DLS-BB044-v.1 and SB-GP_v1. All patients provided written informed consent to Discovery Life Sciences for the research use of their biological samples.  An overview of the experimental design is presented in Fig.  1 . Samples from five patients with colon adenocarcinoma (two males, three females, ages 58–72, pretreatment) were included in this study. From each patient, we included CRC FFPE blocks and NAT blocks for a subset of three patients (bringing the total to eight FFPE blocks), and we obtained paired freshly frozen dissociated tumor cells (for immune profiling analysis), alongside the three selected FFPE blocks used for spatial profiling (Table  1 ).    Tissue sectioning  Adjacent or near-adjacent 5-µm sections were taken from the FFPE tissue blocks following the Xenium In Situ for FFPE — Tissue Preparation Guide ( CG000578 , revision C) for the Xenium workflow or the Visium CytAssist Spatial Gene Expression for FFPE — Tissue Preparation Guide ( CG000518 , revision C) for the Visium workflows.    Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression  H&E staining and imaging were performed following the Visium HD FFPE Tissue Preparation Handbook ( CG000684 ). Samples were then processed and sequenced following the Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kits User Guide ( CG000685 ). Space Ranger version 3.0 was used for analysis. In addition to the native 2-µm feature size, Space Ranger outputs Visium HD data binned to 8-µm and 16-µm resolution. Unless otherwise specified, downstream analyses were performed on the 8-µm resolution data, which provide a 16-fold increase in the average number of UMI reads per bin in the gene–barcode matrix compared to a 2-µm square (Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Performance Technical Note,  CG000686 , revision A), which is of a reasonable size to be processed through third-party tools. Additionally, the 8-µm bin data provide robust cell type annotations (that is, bins are small enough to provide single-cell scale for most cell types). We merged the UMI count matrices of the three sections and, given the dataset's large size, we adopted the sketch-based analysis approach in Seurat ( https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/seurat5_sketch_analysis ), sampling 15% of the entire dataset for downstream analysis  52 , 53  . The 15% sampling rate was chosen to ensure efficient computational performance. We used the leverage score as the sketching method. This method oversamples rare populations to preserve the biological complexity of the sample. We identified variable features, scaled the data, performed principal-component (PC) analysis (PCA) and conducted graph-based clustering (20 PCs, resolution = 0.8). DGE analysis identified cluster marker genes, enabling manual annotation into ten broad cell types (level 1). For level 2 annotations, we reclustered each level 1 cluster (25 PCs, resolution = 0.1) to refine subtypes, performed DGE and annotated cell types. Final annotations were extended to the full dataset.  When needed, the 2 × 2-µm data were used (in combination with nuclear stain) to provide additional information, particularly to locate smaller cell types ( Nuclear segmentation ).    Spatial accuracy  To measure spatial accuracy of mRNA detection, we identified morphologically distinct ROIs and then pinpointed marker genes unique to each ROI. These marker genes should be expressed only in squares directly beneath their corresponding ROI. Using QuPath version 0.4.4 (ref.   54  ), we selected four ROIs within normal colon mucosal glands (hereafter referred to as ‘source masks’) and areas of adjacent muscularis mucosae (‘adjacent masks’), choosing three goblet cell marker genes ( CLCA1 ,  FCGBP  and  MUC2 ). We mapped the locations of all transcripts for these marker genes and calculated the proportion of accurately localized transcripts for each of the four ROIs. For the remaining transcripts, we determined the Euclidean distance from the edge of the nearest source mask to the square of transcript detection. Additionally, we calculated the densities of the marker genes within both the source and adjacent masks for each ROI.    Visium CytAssist Spatial Gene Expression for FFPE  Visium CytAssist Spatial Gene Expression for FFPE (‘Visium v2’) was run on a subset of samples to demonstrate technological improvements of Visium HD. FFPE serial sections (5 µm) were placed on standard glass slides and stained with H&E following the Demonstrated Protocol Visium CytAssist Spatial Gene Expression for FFPE — Deparaffinization, H&E Staining, Imaging & Decrosslinking ( CG000520 ). Samples were processed and sequenced following the Visium CytAssist Spatial Gene Expression Reagent Kits User Guide ( CG000495 ). Space Ranger version 3.0 was used for analysis.    Sensitivity comparison of Visium v2 and Visium HD  We assessed the sensitivity of Visium HD compared to Visium v2 on a gene-by-gene basis. Matched areas were manually selected in Loupe Browser version 8.0, and probe–barcode matrices from each dataset, generated by Space Ranger, were imported into Seurat version 5 (ref.   52  ) using the read10xh5() function. We used the ggplot2 R package to graph per-probe UMI counts. The data were displayed on a log 10  + 1 scale, with Spearman correlations calculated as  r  2 . Our comparison spanned all probes across the entire transcriptome and specifically focused on probes crossing an exon–exon splice junction (7,605 of 54,580 probes). This latter comparison helps exclude most probes that could target gDNA or be susceptible to off-target effects. These probes that are marked as potentially binding to gDNA were excluded from the analysis computationally.  The gDNA estimate is obtained by fitting a piecewise linear model to genes with both spliced and unspliced probes. The model predicts the log-transformed gene counts for unspliced probes as a function of log-transformed gene counts for spliced probes and log-transformed estimated gDNA counts per gene per 1,000 spots under tissue:       x    unspliced    =  gDNA  +  B      x    spliced      −      X    ^      gDNA    II      x    spliced    >      X    ^      gDNA      ,     where X̂ gDNA  is the estimated gDNA UMIs per gene, x unspliced  and x spliced  are the average number of UMIs corresponding to unspliced and spliced probes from a single gene, respectively, and II(      x    spliced    >      X   ˆ     gDNA      ) is an indicator function that equals one if x spliced  is greater than        X   ˆ     gDNA      and zero otherwise.  For any fixed estimate of        X   ˆ     gDNA     , the model parameters gDNA and  B  are estimated by fitting a linear regression with a two-dimensional parameter vector. The relevant        X   ˆ     gDNA      values to consider while fitting the model are only those x spliced  values seen in the genes under consideration. Therefore, a linear model with every x spliced  value seen in the dataset as        X   ˆ     gDNA      is fit, and the model with the smallest residual sum of squares is used for the estimates. For more details on gDNA, see the technical note Visium CytAssist Spatial Gene Expression for FFPE: Robust Data Analysis with Minimal Impact of Genomic DNA ( CG000605 , revision A).    Chromium Single Cell Gene Expression Flex  Cells were dissociated from 50-µm FFPE curls using the Demonstrated Protocol for Isolation of Cells from FFPE Tissue Sections for Chromium Fixed RNA Profiling ( CG000632 ). Library preparation and sequencing followed the Chromium Fixed RNA Profiling for Multiplexed Samples User Guide ( CG000527 , revision D). Cell Ranger version 8.0.0 was used for analysis. To build the atlas, we used Seurat version 5 (ref.   52  ) to import the H5 file produced by the cellranger aggr pipeline. We then plotted the distribution of UMIs and genes per barcode, excluding the top and bottom 2.5% of the distribution to account for outliers. We then used the same sketch approach as the HD data: identified variable features, scaled the data, performed PCA and conducted graph-based clustering (25 PCs, resolution = 0.6) and performed DGE analysis to identify cluster marker genes, enabling manual annotation into ten broad cell types (level 1). For level 2 annotations, we reclustered each level 1 cluster (25 PCs, resolution = 0.1) to refine subtypes, performed DGE and annotated cell types. Final annotations were extended to the full dataset.    Spot deconvolution  Deconvolution methods aim to identify the cell types and their relative proportions contributing to the signal captured in a specific area (spot, square or bin). Spot deconvolution was used to classify and label bins with cell types derived from the Single Cell Atlas. We ran spacexr  55   using doublet mode, which assigns one to two cell types per spot and is recommended for technologies with high spatial resolution such as Visium HD. Among the outputs, this mode provides the top two ranked cell types per spot, a matrix with the weights for all cell types in the reference in each of the spots and a variable representing the class of every bin. The available classes are ‘singlet’ (one cell type), ‘doublet_certain’ (two cell types), ‘doublet_uncertain’ (two cell types, but only confident of one), ‘reject’ (no prediction given). See the spacexr vignette for more detail ( https://raw.githack.com/dmcable/spacexr/master/vignettes/spatial-transcriptomics.html ). Owing to the increased number of barcoded squares in Visium HD, we modified the code to improve runtime ( https://github.com/dmcable/spacexr/pull/206 ). We selected a minimum UMI threshold of 100 for a bin to be considered for the deconvolution step.    Characterizing the tumor periphery  To identify and analyze tumor periphery regions, we developed a custom pipeline ( https://github.com/10XGenomics/HumanColonCancer_VisiumHD ). The key advantage of this method is its versatility; it is not restricted to tumors and can be applied to identify cell types in the boundaries of other tissues, such as colon glands or skeletal muscle tissue. Our algorithm first selects all bins labeled with the given cluster or cell type. For each bin, the algorithm then identifies all neighboring bins within a user-defined radius. We defined this as 50 µm based on biological relevance and to exploit the high resolution of Visium HD. A 50-µm boundary analysis is not possible with Visium v2, which has a spot diameter of 55 µm. To accurately delineate the boundary of the cluster or cell type, the algorithm excludes bins with the same label as the initial bin. To further refine the boundary identification, we removed singlet bins labeled with the given cluster but not in proximity to other bins with the same label. Specifically, we excluded bins that had fewer than 25 neighboring bins with the same label to ensure the selection of well-defined regions within the tissue.  For the macrophage-specific analysis, we selected 8-µm bins that were deconvolved as macrophages and located within 50 µm of tumor regions. For each patient, variable features were identified, the data were scaled and PCA was performed. Graph-based clustering was then conducted using the top ten PCs with a resolution of 0.2. Clusters were annotated based on the expression of  SPP1  and  SELENOP , and an integrated dataset was generated, including only the macrophage subpopulations consistently identified across all sections. To extend this analysis, all bins labeled as macrophages across all sections were included, irrespective of their proximity to the tumor boundary. For this broader dataset, 15 PCs and a resolution of 0.2 were used for clustering to achieve greater resolving power across patients. This approach aimed to determine whether the identified subpopulations were shared across patients or specific to individual patients.    Distance, local and regional analysis  After identifying regions enriched with immune cells, we selected the top three regions exhibiting the highest macrophage density (within bins categorized as tumor tissue) and delineated these areas as ROIs with a radius of 350 µm. Additionally, we identified a ‘cold’ region lacking immune infiltration. To identify genes associated with elevated immune cell density, we used DGE analysis. Subsequent enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes (ranked by log 2  (fold change)) used the Hallmark gene sets linked to specific biological pathways  40   ( https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb/human/genesets.jsp?collection=H ).    Ligand–receptor analysis  To assess cell–cell communication between macrophages and T cells, we used LIANA version 0.1.12, which provides a framework to combine cell communication methods to infer ligand–receptor interactions  33  . We selected all bins within the previously defined tumor periphery region (within 50 µm of the tumor boundary) to create an independent Seurat object to be used as input. We filtered the predicted interactions by selecting any interaction with aggregate_rank ≤ 0.01. This procedure was done on a per-patient basis.    Immune density analysis  To map the locations of specific immune cell types in the CRC samples, we used the coordinates for each bin and their labels provided by deconvolution. We counted only bins that were labeled as singlets. We used 2D kernel density estimation to select regions enriched in a given cell type. Density values were scaled to a maximum of 1.    Nuclear segmentation  Using the 8 × 8-μm binned data for the periphery analysis meant that most T cells in the tumor periphery were assigned to doublet bins or rejected (the algorithm was unable to predict the cell type) and therefore excluded, making them challenging to spatially localize (Fig.  6a  and Extended Data Fig.  8 ). This is an effect of the 8 × 8-μm binned data approach for cell assignment (Fig.  6b ), in which smaller cell types such as T cells (as compared to tumor cells) may colocalize other cell types within the 8 × 8-μm bin. To overcome this, we used an alternative approach to assign 2 × 2-μm squares to cells. We first identified regions enriched in either CD4 +  or CD8 +  T cells, independent of whether they were assigned to a singlet or doublet bin, and, with the use of the nuclear stain from a high-resolution H&E microscope image, we performed nuclear segmentation on these regions. To segment nuclei from the H&E images and assign 2 × 2-µm bins to the identified nuclei, we followed the analysis guide ‘Nuclei Segmentation and Custom Binning of Visium HD Gene Expression Data’ ( https://www.10xgenomics.com/analysis-guides/segmentation-visium-hd ). The segmentation procedure was run on the full section using StarDist  56  . We used affine transformations to preserve the segmentation polygons when subsetting the image to specific ROIs. Once the 2-µm bins were assigned to the corresponding nuclear polygons, the data were transformed to create a gene-by-nucleus UMI count matrix for further processing.    Single-cell immune profiling  Freshly frozen dissociated tumor cells were sorted based on CD45 and CD3 expression to isolate T cells. Gene expression (5′) and TCR libraries were generated and sequenced following the Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 5′ Reagent Kits v2 (Dual Index) User Guide ( CG000331 ). Cell Ranger version 8.0.0 was used for analysis.    Design of TCR clonotype probes  Custom probes for Xenium were developed to target three CDR3 sequences identified by VDJ sequencing (full list of clonotypes in Supplementary Table  4 , probe sequences in Supplementary Table  3 ). One 40-bp probe was designed for each CDR3, centered on the CDR3 with some overhang into the adjacent framework regions. These probes were designed following the specifications in the Species Standalone Custom and Advanced Custom Panel Design for Xenium In Situ Technical Note ( CG000683 , revision C).    Xenium In Situ  The P1CRC, P2CRC and P5CRC samples were processed following the Xenium In Situ Gene Expression with Morphology-based Cell Segmentation Staining User Guide ( CG000749 ) with the Xenium Human Colon Gene Expression Panel (322 genes) supplemented with an additional 100 genes chosen to identify diverse immune populations we observed in the Visium HD data and characterize the TME (for the complete gene list, see Supplementary Table  2 ). The panel was designed using Xenium Panel Designer following the guidance in the Xenium Add-on Panel Design Technical Note ( CG000643 , revision B). The Xenium Onboard Analysis pipeline version 2.0.0 was run directly on the instrument for image processing, cell segmentation, image registration, decoding, deduplication and secondary analysis.
