In addition, we performed pseudo-time analysis based on Palantir [ 25 ] on the RedeFISH-enhanced data, and depicted a transformation trajectory from DCIS #1, DCIS #2, DCIS #3 to invasive tumor cells (Fig.  6 A and Fig.  S10 A), consistent with the fact that DCIS is a preinvasive form of breast cancer [ 26 ]. As expected, DCIS #3 displayed a notably elevated median pseudotime (0.474) in comparison to DCIS #1 (0.198) or DCIS #2 (0.053), and aberrant duct morphology was indicated by the RedeFISH-enhanced data, suggestive of a transitioning state toward an invasive disease. In contrast, DCIS #1 and DCIS #2 were characterized by circular duct-like structures (Fig.  6 A), consistent with the pseudotime analysis results (Fig.  S10 A). Combining pseudotime and DGE analysis,  MDM2  and  DCAF7  exhibited significant up-regulation along the transformation trajectory (Fig.  S10 B), consistent with the recent report of poor prognosis in various types of tumors [ 24 , 27 ]. These genes exhibited significant correlation with tumor development, thereby offering promising potential as biomarkers for investigating how tumor microenvironment changed along the transformation trajectory.  We finally investigated cell type composition in the tumor-adjacent regions and linked the cellular proportion changes with the corresponding pseudotime and the marker genes. Previous studies have shown that the transition from DCIS to invasive tumor cells is accompanied by cellular composition and gene expression alteration [ 28 ]. Our observations indicate that this transition involves a loss of surrounding myoepithelial cells and an increase in vascular endothelial cells, consistent with earlier report [ 26 ] (Fig.  S10 C). In addition, within a 50-μm spatial scale, we observed increased recruitment of macrophages to the invasive tumor site (Fig.  S10 D), which may modulate the tumor microenvironment to further accelerate tumor progression [ 29 ].     Discussion  While imaging-based ST provides unparalleled resolution for dissecting tissue heterogeneity, its utility is often constrained by limited gene recovery and imperfect cell segmentation. To address these challenges, we developed RedeFISH. First, RedeFISH leverages RL to frame cell segmentation as a strategic decision-making problem, iteratively optimizing expression profile similarity to overcome the reliance on staining images in supervised methods and transcript misassignment in unsupervised methods. Second, RedeFISH performs segmentation in a complete transcriptome-driven manner, ensuring optimal alignment of segmented cell expression profiles and enabling whole transcriptome recovery, thus alleviating the limitation of restricted gene detection in imaging-based ST. Third, RedeFISH exhibits broad compatibility across diverse imaging-based ST platforms and, with appropriate preprocessing, is also applicable to sequencing-based ST technologies. Across multiple datasets, RedeFISH yields cell expression profiles that more closely match single-cell references, achieving an average improvement of 9.7% in cosine similarity and a 13.9% reduction in RMSE compared with existing methods. It also improves cell boundary delineation, with an approximately 19% gain over current approaches. In terms of morphology, RedeFISH increases cell area and girth by over 20%, while maintaining roundness at a level comparable to SOTA methods, which may be attributed to its reliance on the spatial distribution of transcripts for morphological inference, introducing inherent uncertainty and stochasticity. By incorporating noise sampling, RedeFISH distinguishes intracellular from extracellular transcripts, accurately delineating cell boundaries in transcript-rich epithelial and immune cell-enriched regions, and achieving robust segmentation even in the highly challenging stromal-enriched areas. Collectively, these results demonstrate that RedeFISH effectively captures the structural organization of diverse tissues, underscoring its robustness for imaging-based ST cell segmentation. Furthermore, they highlight the considerable potential of RL in the analysis of spatial omics data, and we anticipate its broader application in addressing a wide range of challenges in this field.  Integrative analysis of imaging-based ST and scRNA-seq data is pivotal to elucidate spatiotemporal biological processes by resolving the spatial context of gene expression, enabling mechanistic insights into cell–cell interactions and microenvironmental regulation. The deployment of RedeFISH is projected to establish a new standard in spatial omics analysis by synergistically combining the high-plex capability of scRNA-seq with the spatial fidelity of imaging-based ST, ultimately generating biologically interpretable datasets where every measured transcript can be mapped within its native tissue microenvironment while maintaining whole transcriptome breadth. Our application of RedeFISH to mouse ileum dataset revealed a spatially organized  Wnt3 – Fzd5  signaling axis between Paneth cells and intestinal stem cells, mechanistically linking niche topography to stem cell maintenance through ligand–receptor topographic mapping. In human breast cancer specimens, RedeFISH revealed pseudotemporal up-regulation of  MDM2  and  DCAF7  during DCIS-to-invasive transition, coupled with microenvironmental remodeling featuring myoepithelial cell loss and recruitment of macrophages.  Collectively, these results indicate that RedeFISH serves not only as a highly accurate cell segmentation tool but also, through its whole-transcriptome segmentation outputs, facilitates a broad spectrum of downstream analyses, thereby substantially enhancing the application and interpretability of ST data across diverse biomedical research contexts, ranging from fundamental studies of developmental biology to translational investigations in oncology.    Methods   Model overview  RedeFISH leverages a policy gradient-based deep RL framework to perform cell segmentation in imaging-based ST and scRNA-seq data by optimizing expression similarity between ST-derived segments and single-cell transcriptomes. The pipeline begins with data preprocessing to meet the input requirements of the neural network. A segmentation module and a deconvolution module are then implemented to assign transcripts and align single cells within segmented regions. RedeFISH iteratively alternates between these 2 modules over predefined epochs, producing a set of candidate cell segments. Finally, postprocessing refines the segmentation by defining polygonal cell boundaries and imputing whole-transcriptome expression profiles for the segmented cells.    Preprocessing  For data preprocessing, RedeFISH first encodes all molecules into integers. Consider an imaging-based ST dataset containing  n  molecules with spatial coordinates { x i  ,  y i  } and associated genes { g i  }, where  i  = 1,..., n , together with an scRNA-seq expression matrix  U  of dimensions  s  ×  m , representing  s  cells and  m  genes. We assign a unique identifier to each gene in the set  K , which comprises  k  intersection genes { k i  ,  i  = 1,..., k } detected in both scRNA-seq and imaging-based ST. Accordingly, we use positive integers 1 to  k  to represent all genes in  K . For ST data, each molecule is encoded using its corresponding identifier if  g i   ⊆ { k i  }, and otherwise assigned the value  k  + 1. For scRNA-seq data, we construct a new expression matrix  S  of dimensions  s  ×  k , representing the  s  cells and  k  intersection genes.  Next, in order to calculate noise distance scores  NDS i  i  = 1,.., n  for molecules, we implement a k-d tree structure using the Scipy package in Python to find top  d th nearest neighbors for each molecule based on Euclidean distance metric. Then, for each molecule, mean distance  d i  ,  i  = 1,.., n  of the  d th nearest neighbors are determined and the noise distance scores are calculated as:   (1)        NDS  i   =  ReLU    1  −   d  i   /  Q   d    q       i  =  1  ,  …  ,  n  ;  q  ⊂   0  1         where  Q  is quantile function and ReLU represents rectified linear unit activation function. This score measures the distance between a molecule and its  d th nearest neighboring molecules. Hence, a molecule with a low distance score, which signifies a greater separation from other molecules, enhances the likelihood of being classified as background noise within the Segmentation Module.    Segmentation Module  The primary objective of the Segmentation Module is to perform molecule-level classification, ultimately yielding cell regions and aggregating molecules with identical classifications to construct expression profiles. In practice, an ST dataset may contain hundreds of thousands of cells (denoted as  c ), making it impractical to perform  c -classification for each molecule when  c  is extremely large. However, given a list of candidate cells with spatial locations { X i  ,  Y i  },  i  = 1,..., c , RedeFISH identifies top  m th nearest candidate cells and performs an  m -classification for each molecule, where  m  is much smaller than  c . The list of candidate cell locations could be estimated by RedeFISH (see “Estimate candidate cell locations”) or any other algorithm- or experiment-based methods, such as clustering or staining. These methods provide prior estimates of cell center locations, which are used for the initial iteration of RedeFISH. In addition, we define and randomly initialize a  p -dimensional trainable vector  f  for each candidate cell, as well as a  p -dimensional trainable vector  g  for each gene. For a pair of molecular  i  and one of its nearest candidate cell  j , a location vector representing relative position is generated using  Eq. (2) . Postprocessing  Following the final assignment of molecules and the determination of cellular expression profiles, postprocessing is performed to delineate polygonal cell boundaries and impute whole-transcriptome expression profiles for the identified cells. RedeFISH first utilizes the alphashape algorithm in Python to determine polygonal regions of cell bodies, followed by the refinement of molecular assignments based on the results of the alphashape analysis to generate final expression profiles. Then, a matrix  A  was computed to represent the pairwise cosine similarity of log expression between cells in the scRNA-seq data and the output of RedeFISH. For each cell in the output, RedeFISH identifies the  r th most similar cells based on matrix  A . Additionally, for each cell in the scRNA-seq dataset, RedeFISH calculates the occurrence of single cells ( O ) that are present among the  r th most similar cells. Assuming that there are  n  cells in the RedeFISH output, the occurrence scores ( OS ) for single cell  j  are defined in Eq. (19).   (19)    OS  j   =  log    n  /   O  j       For cell  i  in the RedeFISH output, we calculate chosen weights for the  r th most similar single cells by multiplying the expression similarity with corresponding occurrence scores. Thus, we generate a new matrix  W  with  n  ×  r  dimensions by sorting the chosen weights in descending order for each cell. Finally, we impute the whole-transcriptome expression profile for each cell by performing a weighted average of the expression profiles, utilizing the top  k  single cells and their corresponding weights in  W .    Model implement  At the beginning, RedeFISH preforms data preprocessing (see “Preprocessing”) to encode molecules in ST data and generate expression matrix of intersection genes for scRNA-seq data. To initialize the 2 modules, RedeFISH assigns molecules to their nearest candidate cells and generates an expression matrix for the initial assignments and the initial values of  ER ,  ES , and  ESS  are then determined. After that, the model undergoes iteration for a predetermined number of epochs. During each epoch, RedeFISH first employs a batch training strategy to compute the rewards for each molecule, followed by the minimization of region loss based on these rewards. This results in the acquisition of a cell segmentation outcome for each epoch within the Segmentation Module. Next, in Deconvolution Module, RedeFISH updates  ESS  and minimize alignment loss. The  ESS  obtained from the previous epoch is utilized to compute rewards in the Segmentation Module for the next epoch. After completing all epochs, RedeFISH carries out an additional Segmentation Module to determine the final molecular assignments. In this scenario, dropout layers are omitted, and molecular assignments and noise classifications are determined by selecting the maximum probabilities within categorical distributions, rather than employing a sampling approach. In the end, RedeFISH conducts the postprocessing (see the previous section) for generating polygonal regions and imputing whole-transcriptome expression profiles.  To train the RedeFISH model, Adam is selected as the optimizer and exponential learning rate schedule is applied with a multiplicative factor decay of 0.996 for one epoch. The number of epochs was set to a default of 500, with the initial learning rates established at 0.01 for the noise feature matrix and 0.002 for other variables, respectively. In preprocessing,  d  and  q  are set to 100 and 0.999, respectively, for calculating the distance scores. In Segmentation Module, we set  m  = 8 for cell assignments and  p  = 20 for dimensions of cell features and gene features. Additionally, batch size is set to the number of molecules divided by 50 with a maximum value of 2,000,000. In Deconvolution Module, we set  cs  = 10 and the number of iterations in each epoch to 30. In postprocessing,  r  is set to 40 and  k  is set to 20 for imputation of expression profiles. The manuscript consistently employs these default parameters across all experiments, unless otherwise specified in particular notifications.    Estimate candidate cell locations  The purpose of the estimate candidate cell locations step is to generate a set of prior candidate cell center locations for the initial iteration of RedeFISH. To achieve this, we utilize a 3-step approaches, including (a) identifying marker genes based on scRNA-seq data, (b) performing clustering of marker genes based on spatial distribution of corresponding molecules, and (c) clustering molecules into candidate cells for each category of marker gene.  We first identify marker genes for each cell type in the normalized scRNA-seq data. For gene  i  within cell type  j , the average expression levels ( A ij  ) are calculated and the percentage expression ( P ij  ) is determined by dividing the average expression by the total average expression of that gene. Thus, we generate score matrix ( S ij  ) for genes and cell types using  Eq. (20) .   (20)    S   i  ,  j    =  log     A   i  ,  j    +  1    ×   P   i  ,  j      The top  p  marker genes are selected for each cell type based on the descending order of corresponding columns in the score matrix. By eliminating duplicate marker genes, we ultimately obtained a list of  m  unique marker genes.  Next, we perform clustering based on the spatial distribution of the unique marker genes. Given a prior cell radius  r , a grid is generated with a spacing of 2 r  and a total number of  n  nodes. We then calculate  m -dimensional vectors by counting the marker genes located within a radius of    2  r  /   π     adjacent to the nodes to represent features of the nodes, thereby generating a feature matrix  F  with dimension of  m  ×  n . The feature matrix is further standardized by columns. In addition, an  m  ×  m  dimensional similarity matrix  s  is generated by calculating pairwise Pearson’s correlation coefficient between each pair of rows in  F . Based on the similarity matrix, we employ AgglomerativeClustering function in sklearn to cluster  m  unique marker genes into  c  categories. For each category, we generate a threshold expression vector  t  by selecting the maximum expression value of the corresponding gene in  A  and summing these values.  To generate candidate cell locations, we employ the DBSCAN and  K -means algorithms for clustering molecules within each category, and subsequently apply the Mean Shift algorithm to integrate the category-level outcomes and derive the final candidate cells. In detail, we first ascertain the total number of corresponding molecules  h  located in the adjacent area of each node for each category. After that, we define valid nodes by determining whether  h  exceeds the cutoff established in  Eqs. (21)  and  (22) . Next, DBSCAN function in sklearn is applied for unsupervised clustering molecules into categories with parameter eps = 2 r . Based on the outcomes,  K -means is then employed to cluster the molecules in each category into candidate cell and to generate candidate cell locations by averaging the coordinate of molecules for each candidate cell. To implement the candidate cell location estimation process, the parameter  p  for number of marker genes for each cell type is set to 3 and the parameter  c  for the number of marker gene categories is set to 10. Meanwhile,  q  in equation is set to 0.9. The parameter  r  for the prior cell radius is determined based on the resolution of ST and is typically maintained at 6.5 μm.    RedeFISH with nuclear boundary priors  Current imaging-based ST platforms routinely provide nuclear segmentation results. RedeFISH is naturally suited for inferring cell boundaries based on these nuclear segmentations. During the RL stage, the distance from transcripts to the cell center in  Eq. (2)  is replaced with the distance from transcripts to the nuclear region, with distances set to zero for transcripts located inside the nucleus. In the postprocessing stage, after obtaining cell boundaries using alphashapes as described in the “Postprocessing” section, any regions overlapping with other nuclear regions are removed. The resulting cell boundaries are then combined with the prior nuclear boundaries to derive the final cell regions and corresponding expression matrices. Gene imputation is subsequently performed following the procedure described in the “Postprocessing” section.    Datasets for benchmarking

Implement RedeFISH on datasets  We first processed the scRNA-seq data acquired from various sources. For Human-NSCLC dataset, we used the annotation from “cell_type_major” in the h5ad file that includes 24 major cell types. Next, we estimated candidate cell locations for each dataset using the approaches in “Estimate candidate cell locations”. Specifically, the prior cell radius  r  was set to 36, 6.5, 30, 6.5, 13, and 6.5 for Human-NSCLC (CosMx), Human Breast Cancer (Xenium), Mouse Ileum (MERFISH), Mouse Brain (MERSCOPE), Mouse Brain (Stereo-seq), and Mouse Liver (MERSCOPE) datasets, respectively. In addition, we set the number of marker gene categories  c  to 4 for Mouse Brain (MERSCOPE) and Mouse Brain (Stereo-seq) datasets. Finally, based on the estimated candidate cells, RedeFISH was performed for cell segmentation and gene imputation using the same radius ( r ) as defined above and other default parameters.  The Human Lung Cancer (Xenium) dataset includes GT cell boundaries. Following a strategy similar to that used in Proseg, we used the Xenium output as prior information. Specifically, the nuclear boundaries provided by Xenium were used as priors, and cell boundaries were inferred using the procedure described in the “RedeFISH with Nuclear Boundary Priors” section. The cell radius parameter  r  was set to 6.5, with all other parameters kept at their default settings.  By exception, a different preprocessing procedure was performed for the Mouse Brain (Stereo-seq) dataset, which is based on sequencing-based ST platforms. We initially derived a list of molecules with spatial coordinates by transforming the spot-by-gene expression matrix into an imaging-based format, wherein each sequencing-based unique molecular identifier (UMI) was treated as a discrete molecule. Then, top 2000 intersection genes, exhibiting the highest levels of expression in ST data, were identified and subsequently encoded as positive integers from 1 to 2000, whereas other genes were encoded as 2001. After that, candidate cell estimation and RedeFISH were performed, with the quantile  q  set to 0.9999 in RedeFISH.    Implement Baysor on datasets  We implemented Baysor v0.5.0 [ 11 ] on the benchmarking datasets. Firstly, we used “--save-polygons GeoJSON” to generate polygonal regions of segmented cells. Then, the scale parameter was set to 50, 7, 6.5, 30, and 9 for Human-NSCLC (CosMx), Human Breast Cancer (Xenium), Human Lung Cancer (Xenium), Mouse Ileum (MERFISH), and Mouse Brain (MERSCOPE) datasets, respectively, to maintain an approximately equivalent cellular radius between segmented cells from Baysor or original publication. In addition, the implementation of Baysor is infeasible for ultra-large datasets, such as Mouse Liver and Mouse Brain (Stereo-seq) datasets, due to memory limitation (exceed 5 TB).    Implement Proseg on datasets  We analyzed the Human-NSCLC (CosMx), Human Breast Cancer (Xenium), Mouse Liver (MERSCOPE), Human Lung Cancer (Xenium), and Mouse Brain (MERSCOPE) datasets using Proseg v2.0.4 [ 13 ]. The preliminary transcript assignment results and transcript information provided with these datasets were input into Proseg, and analyses were performed with default parameters. The Mouse Ileum (MERFISH) dataset was excluded because the preliminary transcript assignment results were not available, and the Mouse Brain (Stereo-seq) dataset was not included as it is a sequencing-based ST platform.    Implement Cellpose-SAM on datasets  We used the Cellpose package (v4.0.8) in Python, which implements the Cellpose-SAM model [ 17 ], to analyze the Human Breast Cancer (Xenium), Mouse Brain (MERSCOPE), and Human Lung Cancer (Xenium) datasets. For the Human Breast Cancer (Xenium) dataset, H&E-stained images were used as input to obtain nuclear mask matrices. For the Mouse Brain (MERSCOPE) and Human Lung Cancer (Xenium) datasets, 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI)-stained images were used as input to generate nuclear mask matrices. The nuclear boundaries were then expanded outward by up to 5 μm or until reaching the boundary of neighboring cells to derive the cell mask matrices. Based on these masks, polygon coordinates of cell boundaries and corresponding cellular expression profiles were obtained. All parameters were kept at their default settings.    Implement Stardist on datasets  We used StarDist (v0.9.2) to analyze the Human Breast Cancer (Xenium), Mouse Brain (MERSCOPE), and Human Lung Cancer (Xenium) datasets. The input data and postprocessing steps were identical to those used for Cellpose-SAM, and all parameters were kept at their default settings.    Expression similarity  As one goal of RedeFISH is to optimize expression profiles of segmented cells, we measured expression similarity between segmented cells and single cells in scRNA-seq data. To achieve this, cosine similarity and root mean square error (RMSE) were calculated as evaluation metrics for assessing the similarities. We firstly identified the intersection genes between ST and scRNA-seq data, subsequently generating expression matrices  A  and  B  based on the shared genes. The total UMI counts of each cell in  A  and  B  were additionally normalized to the total number of the intersection genes. Thus, given a segmented cell  i  and single cell  j , the corresponding cosine similarity ( SIM_COS   i , j  ) and RMSE ( SIM_RMSE   i , j  ) were computed as:   (24)       SIM  _   COS   i  ,  j    =  CosineSimilarity    A  i      B  j            (25)   SIM  _   RMSE   i  ,  j    =     1  k   ∑      A  i   −   B  j     2       where  k  refers to number of the intersection genes. For each segmented cell  i , we generated 2 lists of similarities between  i  and all single cells, therefore { SIM_COS   i ,1 , ...,  SIM_COS   i , n  } and { SIM_RMSE   i ,1 ,..., SIM_RMSE   i , n  }. Finally, overall similarities  SIM_C i   and  SIM_R i   were calculated by averaging the top 20 highest values from the first list and the top 20 lowest values from the second list, respectively. We compared  SIM_C  and  SIM_R  for all identified cells across the 3 approaches using boxplot and the Wilcoxon test across 6 datasets. A higher  SIM_C  and a lower  SIM_R  indicate an enhanced level of expression similarity between segmented cells and single cells. The corresponding scRNA-seq data used for similarity calculations in this section are provided in the “Datasets for benchmarking” section.    Boundary alignment  To assess the agreement between segmented cells and GT boundaries, we evaluated both sensitivity and specificity on Human Lung Cancer (Xenium) dataset. For sensitivity, each GT cell was matched to its nearest segmented cell and their regional overlap was measured. For specificity, each segmented cell was matched to its nearest GT cell. Agreement between regions was quantified using the IoU, defined as the ratio of the intersection area to the union area. To estimate cell morphological similarity, we firstly used the Python package Shapely (v2.1.2) to compute the area  s  and girth  c  of each segmented cell, and calculated roundness  R  according to the following formula:   (26)   R  =  4  π  s  /   c  2     Then, we plotted the density curves of morphological features for segmented cells from each method and the GT cells, and computed the IoU between the areas under the corresponding curves to assess the consistency of cell morphology.    Imputation accuracy  To assess imputation accuracy, 30% of genes were randomly masked in the Human-NSCLC (CosMx), Human Breast Cancer (Xenium), Mouse Liver (MERSCOPE), Mouse Brain (MERSCOPE), and Mouse Ileum (MERFISH) datasets. RedeFISH was applied using the remaining 70% of genes to perform cell segmentation and gene expression imputation. The similarity between the imputed expression and the original expression of the masked genes was then computed as described in the “Expression similarity” section. This procedure was repeated 3 times for each dataset.    Evaluation of the impact of the noise sampling step  To evaluate the impact of noise sampling on cell segmentation in RedeFISH, we simulated a variant without noise sampling by setting the probability of assigning molecules to non-noise categories in  Eq. (7)  to a constant value of 1, and fixing the  NDS  score in  Eq. (9)  to 1, while keeping all other components of RedeFISH unchanged. We then ran this modified version on the Human Lung Cancer (Xenium) dataset and assessed its effect on cell segmentation from both cellular region and morphological perspectives. Specifically, following the procedure described in “Boundary alignment,” we computed the relevant metrics and compared the statistical results with and without the noise sampling step.    Runtime efficiency  We compared the runtime efficiency of RedeFISH, Baysor, and Proseg on the Human-NSCLC (CosMx), Human Breast Cancer (Xenium), Mouse Liver (MERSCOPE), Mouse Brain (MERSCOPE), Mouse Ileum (MERFISH), and Human Lung Cancer (Xenium) datasets. RedeFISH was executed using a single NVIDIA RTX 5880 Ada GPU. For Baysor and Proseg, which are central processing unit (CPU)-based methods, the maximum number of threads was set to 16.    Label transfer  To facilitate comparison of cell type distributions, we applied label transfer to automatically assign cell types from scRNA-seq data to segmented cells. For each cell, the top 20 scRNA-seq cells with the highest cosine similarity in expression profiles were identified. The similarity scores were then aggregated by cell type and normalized by the total similarity across the 20 cells, yielding a probability distribution of cell type assignments. The cell type with the highest probability was designated as the final identity of each cell.  We performed label transfer on the cell segmentation results obtained from RedeFISH, Baysor, Proseg, and the original studies to automatically assign cell types and to compare differences in cell type distributions across approaches.    Analysis of mouse ileum dataset  We applied Leiden for cell clustering based on the expression profiles of identified cells, followed by manual cell annotation using marker genes. Then, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (tSNE) in Scanpy packages was applied for cell type illustration. Recently, numerous algorithms have been developed for analyzing cell–cell interactions [ 35 , 36 ]. We employed CellPhoneDB to assess the significance of interactions between  Wnt  and  Fzd–Lrp  complexes.    Analysis of human breast cancer dataset  Initially, Leiden combined with manual annotation was employed for the purpose of cell type annotation. Based on the spatial distribution of cell types, 4 ROIs were selected for downstream analysis, namely, DCIS #1, DCIS #2, DCIS #3, and invasive tumor. To investigate up-regulated genes in ROIs, we randomly selected 300 cells from one ROI and 100 cells from each of the remaining 3 ROIs, which was designated as the control group. Then, edgeR [ 37 ] was applied to identify up-regulated genes and compute the level of statistical significance. In addition, we used GEPIA [ 22 ] to analyze survival rate for several genes. In this analysis, we chose BRCA HER2 +  nonluminal dataset, because the tissue block was annotated as HER2 + /ER + /PR − , and set 60% and 40% for parameter Cutoff-High and Cutoff-Low, respectively. For pseudotime analysis, we randomly chose one start cell and 3 terminal cells from DCIS #1 and invasive tumor ROIs, respectively, and applied Palantir [ 25 ] with default setting for estimating pseudotime for DCIS and invasive tumor cells. We further employed a smooth spline method to perform curve fitting between pseudotime and gene expressions or cell type proportions.  To investigate cell type proportions in tumor microenvironment, for each ROI, we first generated a spatial coordinate list corresponding to the cell types of interest within that ROI. For example, in the DCIS #1 ROI, this corresponds to a list of spatial coordinates for DCIS #1 cells. Subsequently, we identified all cells located within a specified radius (10, 20, 50, and 100 μm) of any cell in the spatial coordinate list and calculated the cell type proportions based on the identified cells.    AI-assisted graphical elements generation  Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted tools (Doubao AI) were used to generate certain graphical elements in Fig.  1 B. The authors reviewed and edited all outputs. evidence_text: Iron-catalyzed oxidative stress reveals an exposome-related ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic niche in BRCA1-linked renal carcinogenesis. Early cancer initiation under chronic oxidative stress requires the survival of epithelial cells that should otherwise be eliminated by regulated cell death. However, the spatial and morphological identity of such stress-adapted cells remains poorly defined. Here, we integrated Xenium single-cell spatial transcriptomics, quantitative nuclear morphometrics, mitochondrial analyses, and human cancer datasets to investigate iron-driven renal carcinogenesis in Brca1(L63X/+) rats. Ferric nitrilotriacetate exposure induced dynamic remodeling of proximal tubular epithelium, characterized by loss of homeostatic transport and mitochondrial programs, and activation of Myc, Met, Lcn2, Anxa2 and iron-handling genes. BRCA1 haploinsufficiency expanded a karyomegalic proximal tubular state associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, chromatin hyperchromasia, nuclear remodeling, and ferroptosis-resistant transcriptional features. Subclassification of karyomegalic cells identified distinct stress-adaptive populations, including a BRCA1-associated K2 state enriched for Myc/Met/Lcn2 signaling and preferentially embedded within a pro-oncogenic epithelial-stromal microenvironment. Of note, neighboring non-karyomegalic proximal tubular cells acquired related iron-handling and survival-biased programs, indicating that karyomegaly marks a broader pre-neoplastic field rather than an isolated abnormality. Human TCGA renal cancer analyses and morphometric assessment of BRCA1-mutant breast tissue further supported the clinical relevance of karyomegaly-associated gene modules and nuclear remodeling. These findings define a spatially organized, ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic niche as an early lesion in iron-driven carcinogenesis and establish quantitative nuclear morphology as a functional readout of exposome-related oxidative stress adaptation in genetically susceptible tissues. mutant) rat     n.s.   not significant     NSD   nuclear substructure density     OA_PT    oxidative stress–adaptive  proximal tubule     OCR   oxygen-consumption rate     PCA   principal component analysis     PFI   progression-free interval     PII   peripheral intensity index     PT   proximal tubule (tubular cell[s])     RCA   rolling circle amplification     RCC   renal cell carcinoma     REF   rat embryonic fibroblast     ROI   region of interest     ssGSEA   single-sample gene set enrichment analysis     ST   stromal cell(s)     STN   solid tissue normal (non-tumorous portion)     TA   tissue array     TCGA   The Cancer Genome Atlas     TEM   transmission electron microscopy     TR_PT    transient regenerative  proximal tubule     UMAP   uniform manifold approximation and projection     WSI   whole slide image (imaging)     WT   wild-type       1  Introduction  Iron is essential for life [ 1 ], yet its redox activity also drives oxidative reactions that promote mutagenesis and malignant transformation [ 2 , 3 ]. Although persistent oxidative stress is increasingly recognized as a trigger of tumor initiation, how damaged epithelial cells survive this hostile redox environment and acquire tumor-initiating potential remains poorly understood. We previously established a ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA) model of Fenton reaction–driven carcinogenesis that reproducibly induces metastatic renal adenocarcinomas and enables mechanistic analysis of oxidative stress–mediated tumorigenesis [ [4] ,  [5] ,  [6] ]. However, the spatially organized molecular programs that allow a subset of injured epithelial cells to evade elimination and persist as pre-neoplastic precursors have not been defined.  Hereditary cancers account for 5–10% of human malignancies [ 7 , 8 ]. Among hereditary cancer genes,  BRCA1  and  BRCA2  are best known for their association with breast and ovarian cancers [ 9 ], but growing evidence suggests broader roles in epithelial cancer susceptibility, including renal cell carcinoma [ 10 , 11 ]. We recently established Brca1/2 haploinsufficient rat models that recapitulate key aspects of human disease [ [12] ,  [13] ,  [14] ]. Notably, Fe-NTA–induced carcinogenesis is markedly accelerated in Brca1 haploinsufficient rats and accompanied by recurrent  c-Myc  amplification and mitochondrial abnormalities during early tumorigenesis [ 15 , 16 ]. These findings raise the possibility that BRCA1 deficiency promotes the emergence of stress-adaptive epithelial states that evade ferroptotic elimination during tumor initiation.  Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics enable single-cell–resolution molecular profiling while preserving tissue architecture and histological context [ 17 ]. Here, we integrated Xenium-based spatial transcriptomics with quantitative digital nuclear morphometrics to investigate early carcinogenic processes under iron-driven oxidative stress. This approach identified a previously unrecognized ferroptosis-resistant karyomegalic epithelial population associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, oncogenic signaling, and iron-handling programs. Integration with human cancer datasets further suggested that related stress-adaptive programs and nuclear abnormalities may be relevant to human epithelial tumorigenesis. Together, our findings establish a spatial and morphological framework for understanding how exposome-related [ 18 ] oxidative stress intersects with hereditary susceptibility during the earliest stages of tumor initiation.    2  Materials and methods   2.1  Renal carcinogenesis model by ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA)  All the animal experiments were approved by the animal experimental committee of Nagoya University Graduate School of Medicine.  Sprague-Dawley  strain male rats of wild-type (WT) and  Brca1(L63X/+ ; mutant, MUT) [ 12 ] were bred as described previously [ 15 ]. Representative kidney specimens of 1 and 3 weeks under the carcinogenesis protocol were obtained and fixed either in phosphate-buffered 10% formalin for 48 h for paraffin-embedding, or 2 % glutaraldehyde in 1 mM phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for resin-embedding.    2.2  Tissue array construction  Six formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) rat kidney samples were organized into a tissue array (TA) format to enable simultaneous Xenium processing (three samples per slide; two slides per instrument run). RNA quality was pre-verified by RNAScope in situ on the sections from all the donor blocks. After confirmation, sample area was selected and manually extracted to re-form new TA blocks with samples coring within proper size of area (∼12 mm × 24 mm). From each TA block, 5 μm sections were cut with a rotary microtome (Leica RM2135) and mounted onto  Xenium  adhesive slides (10x Genomics). Sections were dried overnight, then stored in a desiccator until processing. All cutting and mounting steps were performed with precautions to maintain tissue morphology and RNA integrity (sterile, RNase-free tools and surfaces).    2.3  Gene panel design  A custom 50-gene  Xenium In Situ  probe panel (ID:  TCMFHM ) was designed for  Rattus norvegicus  using the 10x Genomics Custom Panel Designer ( Table S1 ). Target genes were selected to represent major renal cell types and key kidney injury pathways, prioritizing established marker genes for nephron segments (proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct principal/intercalated cells), glomerular cell types (podocytes, endothelial), interstitial cells (stromal cells), immune infiltrates (inflammatory cells), and urothelium, alongside transcripts implicated in our previous differential expression array analyses [ 15 , 19 , 20 ]. Gene selection was further guided by a published rat kidney single-cell transcriptomic atlas (E-GEAD-450 [ 21 ]), retaining only genes with robust, cell type-specific expression in the reference dataset. The final panel included renal biomarkers and ferroptosis-, oncogenic/tumor suppressor-, mitochondria-associated genes relevant to renal pathophysiology [ 15 , 22 ]. Probes were tiled across exonic regions with high specificity, minimizing off-target homology and maximizing RNA accessibility; negative control and decoding control probes were included for quality control [ 23 ].    2.4  Xenium in situ workflow  FFPE tissue sections (5 μm) were processed using the Xenium FFPE in situ transcriptomics protocol (10x Genomics, v1.0; Demonstrated Protocol  CG000580 ;  Fig. 1 A). Briefly, sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated, subjected to antigen retrieval and RNA exposure, and enzymatically digested under RNase-free conditions to facilitate probe penetration while preserving tissue morphology. Probe hybridization was performed at 50 °C for approximately 18 h. After stringent washes, adjacently hybridized probe pairs were ligated for 2 h at 37 °C and amplified by rolling circle amplification (RCA) for 2 h at 30 °C to generate detectable signals [ 24 ]. Tissue autofluorescence was reduced by chemical quenching, and nuclei were counterstained with DAPI for visualization and segmentation. Processed slides were mounted in Xenium imaging buffer, sealed in Xenium cassettes, and stored at 4 °C in the dark until analysis.  Fig. 1   Xenium in situ enables spatially resolved single-cell atlas of the rat kidney with customized gene panel.  A,  Experimental workflow: Wild-type (WT) and  Brca1 -mutant (MUT) rats received ferric nitrilotriacetate (Fe-NTA) treatment and were dissected at the indicated time-points (control, 1 week, 3 weeks) to obtain kidneys. Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) sections were processed on the Xenium platform. Following in-situ transcript capture and high-plex imaging, the identical sections were stained with H&E to provide histological context (Scale bars, 10 μm).  B , UMAP embedding of Xenium-profiled cells from the WT control kidney, marked by cell-type annotation derived from canonical marker genes ( Table S1 ).  C,  Dot-plot of the top markers per cell type. Circle size indicates the percentage of nuclei expressing the gene; color denotes mean of normalized expression (z-scored).  D,  WT control renal cortex: H&E image overlaid with Xenium-decoded cells colored by cell-type annotation in B (scale bar, 100 μm).                        2.4.1  Xenium analyzer instrument  Automated imaging and transcript decoding were performed on the 10x Genomics Xenium Analyzer using software v2.0.1.0. The instrument acquired high-resolution images through 15 iterative cycles of fluorescent probe binding, imaging, and signal removal. Four fluorescent channels were used per cycle, allowing each gene in the custom panel to be identified by a unique optical barcode. Images were acquired at 200 nm/pixel resolution with a 20× objective, and Z-stack images were collected at 0.75 μm intervals. Adjacent fields of view were tiled and computationally stitched using DAPI nuclear signals as fiducial landmarks to generate a registered whole-tissue image.  Transcripts were decoded by matching fluorescent puncta to the predefined barcode codebook. Only transcripts with a Q-score ≥20, corresponding to approximately 99% decoding accuracy, were retained for downstream analysis [ 23 ]. Detected transcripts were exported with XY coordinates, gene identities, and Q-scores. Negative-control probe signals accounted for <0.03% of total reads, indicating low background noise.    2.4.2  Cell segmentation and transcript assignment  Cell segmentation was performed using the Xenium onboard segmentation pipeline. DAPI images were used to identify nuclear boundaries, which were expanded isotropically by up to 15 μm or until they reached neighboring cell boundaries. This nuclear expansion method generated non-overlapping cell polygons approximating renal epithelial cell boundaries. Decoded transcripts located within each polygon were assigned to the corresponding cell, producing a cell-by-gene expression matrix for downstream single-cell spatial analysis [ 23 ].    2.4.3  Post-Xenium histology  After transcript profiling, the same tissue sections were re-stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) to correlate molecular data with tissue morphology. H&E images were acquired using a Leica Aperio AT2 slide scanner at 40× magnification and processed in QuPath 0.5.1 to generate OME-TIFF files. The H&E images were then aligned to DAPI images in Xenium Explorer, allowing transcript-defined cell types and spatial regions to be evaluated in relation to histological structures, such as glomeruli and renal tubules.     2.5  Bioinformatic analysis of spatial transcriptomics data   2.5.1  Data preprocessing and normalization  Xenium outputs (six rat kidney FFPE tissue samples: WT_CT, MUT_CT, WT_Fe1w, MUT_Fe1w, WT_Fe3w, MUT_Fe3w) were loaded into R (version 4.4.1) and converted to a Seurat object using Seurat v5.0.1. All data normalization was performed by SCTransform to stabilize variance transformation and to regress out sequencing-depth effects. This yielded log-normalized count data (stored in Seurat “SCT” assay) for each sample, mitigating technical variability while preserving biological variation. Low-quality cells (e.g. with extremely low transcript counts) were minimal due to Xenium's preprocessing and only cells with nCount_Xenium >0 were retained.    2.5.2  Data integration and clustering  Following normalization, the unified object containing data from six samples was processed for joint analysis. We re-ran SCTransform (merged), PCA (all genes; 30 PCs), FindNeighbors (dims 1–30), FindClusters (resolution 2.0), and UMAP (PCA), which yielded multiple clusters with distinct transcriptional signatures. Mixing across samples in PCA/UMAP was inspected to verify minimal batch effects. Clusters were manually annotated to kidney lineages (proximal tubule, stromal, endothelial, loop of Henle, collecting duct principal/intercalated, podocyte, inflammatory, proximal-like) based on canonical markers [ 21 ] and spatial context provided by Xenium Explorer. For focused analyses, we subset proximal_tubules and stromal_cells contents and re-ran the same pipeline on (i) the merged dataset to confirm lineage assignments and (ii) each compartment separately to resolve fine subclusters (pt_n; st_n) for downstream analyses.    2.5.3  Pathological score maps  Proximal-tubule clusters were defined into four pathology groups by expressional signatures and tubular morphology: normal_tubules (PT_1,2,5,6,10,11), acute_injured (PT_8), subacute_injured (PT_0,3,4,7), and dying_tubules (PT_9). Using Seurat v5.0.1 we set group identities and performed one-vs-rest DE per group with FindMarkers (two-sided Wilcoxon; min.pct = 0.2, logfc.threshold = 0.25, only.pos = TRUE). The top 10 genes by avg_log2FC per group were used for visualization (group-wise AverageExpression heatmap, z-scored by gene). For quantitative per-cell scores, we computed module scores with AddModuleScore on the available marker genes for each group (requiring ≥5 genes), using nbin = 3 and ctrl = 10 to ensure robust background control on the limited panel. Scores were then row-matched by cell_ID and merged into the Giotto (v4.2.0) object's cell_metadata for downstream spatial mapping. All plotting of score maps used fixed global min–max limits per score and unified diverging palettes to enable cross-sample comparison.    2.5.4  Morphological-transcriptomics analysis of nuclei  Nuclear polygons from Xenium segmentation (“nucleus_boundaries.csv.gz”) were imported into R (sf v1.0.19; tidyverse v2.0.0) to compute per-nucleus morphometrics: nuclear area, eccentricity (elongation, 0–1), circularity (4π·area/perimeter 2 ), compactness, convexity, solidity (area/convex hull area) and perimeter/area ratio (boundary irregularity). Polygons were linked to the same cell barcodes used in Seurat; analyses were restricted to proximal tubule cells with expression taken from the SCT assay.  For each gene–feature pair, we fit single-cell linear models per FOV (WT_Fe3w: FOV_3; MUT_Fe3w: FOV_6) with the morphology feature z-scored and technical covariates (library size, detected features) included; slopes (β) and two-sided  P  values were recorded and FDR-adjusted within FOV (Benjamini–Hochberg). As robustness checks, we computed Spearman correlations and ran elastic net models (glmnet) to assess whether multiple features jointly predict expression; a non-zero coefficient denoted feature selection.  To obtain genotype-robust effects, per-FOV slopes were combined by sample-size–weighted averaging (pooled β), and per-FOV  P  values were combined by Stouffer's method (weights ∝ √n), followed by FDR across all pairs. For each gene we derived a “consensus rank” integrating pooled β, pooled FDR, and elastic-net selection.  To identify coordinated programs, each gene was represented by its vector of pooled β across morphology features. Cosine similarity was computed between genes; pairs with similarity ≥0.6 were connected and clustered by Louvain community detection to define morphology-linked gene modules.    2.5.5  Quantification of nuclear phenotypes and integration with transcriptomics  For fields of view (FOVs) from WT_Fe3w (FOV3) and MUT_Fe3w (FOV6), nuclei were segmented using Cellpose (v2.3.2; pretrained nuclei model) [ 37 ]. Three per-cell nuclear morphological readouts were derived from the hematoxylin channel (skimage.color.rgb2hed) within each nuclear mask: (i) hematoxylin optical density (HOD), mean channel intensity following Gaussian smoothing (σ = 0.5 μm); (ii) nuclear substructure density (NSD), the count of intranuclear hematoxylin-dense foci, detected after within-nucleus 2nd-98th percentile normalization, Otsu thresholding, and filtration by area (0.3–6.0 μm 2 ) and circularity (4πA/P 2  ≥ 0.40), expressed per 100 μm 2  of nuclear area; and (iii) peripheral intensity index (PII), (mean        H  O  D   periphery      − mean        H  O  D   interior     )/section-median HOD, where peripheral (distance ≤ s) and interior (distance > s) zones were defined from a Euclidean distance transform of the nuclear boundary at shell thicknesses  s  ∈ (0.5, 1.0, 1.5) μm ( Fig. S4C ); section-median HOD was estimated once per FOV from a random sample of ∼2000 nuclei.  Cellpose-segmented nuclei were assigned Xenium cell identity via two-stage spatial registration. First, an existing QuPath-to-Xenium cell correspondence (established by manual landmark selection and iterative refinement) provided position anchors for an affine transform between the FOV image and Xenium coordinate spaces. Second, true nuclear centroids (QuPath nucleus geometry) were matched to the affine-registered Cellpose nuclei by reciprocal nearest-neighbor matching within the shared coordinate space, at the tightest tolerance (0.5–5 μm ladder) retaining ≥90% of the maximum achievable match count. PT filtering was performed after registration to avoid selection bias. Registration accuracy was confirmed by comparing QuPath's measurements (HOD;  Fig. S4A ) against Cellpose/scikit-image values.    2.5.6  Gene–morphometry association models (HOD/NSD/PII)  For each gene     g     and within a condition (WT_Fe3w; MUT_Fe3w) independently, a single-cell ordinary least-squares model was fitted:     Y  i   =  α  +   β  g   ·   X   i  g    +  γ   A  i   +   ϵ  i     where      Y  i      is the nuclear morphometric readout for cell     i     (HOD; NSD;       P  I  I   s     ),      X   i  g       is the log 1 p-normalized Xenium transcript count for gene     g     in cell     i    , and      A  i      is Cellpose-measured nuclear area (μm 2 ). Two-sided Wald p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons across 50 genes within each condition (Benjamini–Hochberg, FDR <0.05). Cross-condition concordance was assessed by Pearson correlation and sign agreement of per-gene      β  ˆ      between FOVs. Estimates were pooled by fixed-effects inverse-variance weighting:      β  ˆ    F  E    =     ∑  k    w  k     β  ˆ   k      ∑  k    w  k     ,   w  k   =  S   E  k   −  2      with pooled Wald z-statistics BH-FDR corrected across all 50 genes. Models were implemented in Python (statsmodels v0.14; scipy).    2.5.7  Karyomegaly sub-stratification and peri-karyomegaly analysis  PT cells from merged Xenium dataset were defined as karyomegalic (enlarged) if nuclear area > mean+2SD within the PT cell population, and elongated if major/minor axis ratio >2. SCTransform-normalized RNA counts from karyomegalic cells were stored as a SCTx assay. Morphological features processed from nuclear polygons were stored as a MORPH assay and reduced by PCA.  Karyomegalic PTs were then reclustered by a weighted nearest-neighbor (WNN) model that integrates RNA and morphology: SCTx PCA (dims 1–30) and a PCA of z-scored morphology (dims 1–6) were combined with FindMultiModalNeighbors (modality weights recorded as SCTx.weight/MORPH.weight), followed by UMAP on the weighted graph and Louvain communities on wsnn; we grid-searched morphology PCs (2-4, 6) × resolution (0.2, 0.3) and selected the setting with the highest mean silhouette in the WNN UMAP, followed by further resolution tuning, yielding the final result (K0–K5, resolution 0.15). Gene markers were computed using Seurat FindAllMarkers (logistic regression with covariates sample, fov_num, nCount_SCTx). Morphology tiles report per-feature means with significance from two-sided linear models (BH-FDR <0.05).  Spatial context was obtained by overlaying subcluster labels onto H&E in Xenium Explorer (Fe-NTA, 3-week). For peri-karyomegalic analyses, each karyomegalic PT served as a center; PT neighbors within 30 μm were compared with PTs >30 μm away, and hallmark expression visualized as z-scored heatmaps/dot plots (Wilcoxon, BH-FDR where indicated).    2.5.8  Neighborhood composition and microenvironment analysis  Cell centroids (centroid_x, centroid_y) and annotations from the Seurat metadata were filtered to proximal_tubules and stromal_cells, and used for point map plotting and neighbor-associated computations. Independently for each sample, the number of stromal neighbors within a 30 μm Euclidean radius was recorded for each PT cell, by a KD-tree constructed over stromal cell centroids (FNN v1.1.4.1, R; k ≤ 500). Group differences were assessed by Kruskal–Wallis test; pairwise post-hoc comparisons used Dunn's test with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction (rstatix v0.7.3, R). Beyond cell-intrinsic analysis, we modeled proximal-tubule/stromal spatial organization with Giotto (v4.2.0; Python backend) [ 25 ]. For each field, we constructed a radius-based neighbor graph (30 μm) to capture tubulointerstitial contacts in renal tissue [ 26 ]. Community detection on this neighborhood graph using the Leiden algorithm (findNetworkCommunities) yielded microenvironment (ME) clusters, i.e., spatially coherent neighborhoods that may contain mixed PT (pt_n) and stromal (st_n) subtypes. We quantified the cell-type composition and contact enrichment for each ME cluster (normalized by cell abundance). ME prevalences were compared across the six samples to assess genotype/treatment effects. ME labels were overlaid on tissue images in Xenium Explorer to verify anatomic plausibility.  To test whether ME states were independent of karyomegalic clusters, we constructed a WNN-karyomegalic × ME contingency table and applied a Pearson χ 2  test of independence (chisq.test) Tiles in the heatmap display standardized Pearson residuals (Haberman adjustment, chis$stdres): positive (green) indicates over-representation; negative (red) indicates under-representation. Significance stars denote: ∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  1.96    , ∗∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  2.58    , and ∗∗∗ for     ∣   r   i  j    ∣  ≥  3.00    . Global association was summarized by Cramér's     V  =     χ  2   /   (   N   [   min  ⁡   (   r  ,  c   )   −  1   ]    )       ; extremely small P values are reported as thresholds (e.g.,     p  <  2.2  ×   10   −  16      ).    2.5.9  Data visualization  All data visualization was performed in R (v4.4.1), using ggplot2 and plotters bundled with Seurat unless noted otherwise. Low-dimensional embeddings (UMAP) were rendered with DimPlot and annotated by cluster, sample, or FOV; single-gene summaries used VlnPlot or Seurat DotPlot. Heatmaps were produced with ComplexHeatmap for clustered expression/annotation panels and pheatmap for compact correlation/residual matrices. Panel assembly used patchwork/cowplot with harmonized color palettes, fixed aspect ratios for spatial panels, and consistent legends/scales. Multi-panel gene maps ( Fig. 2 C) and pathology-score maps ( Fig. 3 E) were generated in Giotto and exported in R. Xenium Explorer was used only to overlay labels on H&E/DAPI micrographs. Differential expression (DE) used Seurat FindMarkers/FindAllMarkers on SCT-normalized data with two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum tests. Genes were eligible if detected in ≥5% of cells in either group; we report avg_log2FC (positive = higher in the first group), pct_in/pct_out, and adjusted P. Multiple testing was controlled by Benjamini–Hochberg; genes with FDR <0.05 and log 2 FC ≥ 0.25 were considered significant. Random subsampling (set.seed 42) was applied only to downsample points for visualization and was never applied in statistical testing. Box-and-violin plots display median and inter-quartile range; error bars represent 95% confidence intervals unless specified. Because the Xenium dataset included one representative specimen per genotype/treatment condition, cell-level statistics were interpreted as discovery-level measures of spatial association or enrichment rather than animal-level biological replication; key conclusions were supported by prior Fe-NTA data, mitochondrial TEM/REF analyses, and TCGA-based human validation.    2.5.11  Code availability No new algorithms were developed for this manuscript. All code created for analysis is available from the authors upon request.  Mitochondrial cristae morphometry analysis  Transmission electron microscopic images were acquired on a JEM-1400PLUS (JEOL; Tokyo, Japan). Images were analyzed in Fiji/ImageJ (v1.54p). After pixel calibration, individual mitochondria were manually outlined as ROIs with area (μm 2 ) recorded. Within each ROI, cristae ridges were segmented using Trainable Weka Segmentation (Fiji) to obtain a probability map for cristae vs. matrix. High-confidence pixels were thresholded and processed with Ridge Detection to obtain ridge centerlines, followed by Skeletonize (2D/3D) and Analyze Skeleton to quantify branch geometry. Derived per-mitochondrion metrics were: Total cristae length (μm) = Σ branch lengths;  Mean branch length (μm) = Σ branch lengths / number of branches;  Cristae length density (μm/μm 2 ) = total cristae length / mitochondrial area.   Metrics were exported as CVS files and plotted in R.    2.7  Immunoblotting  Kidney cortex lysates were prepared in RIPA buffer, resolved by SDS–PAGE and transferred by standard methods. Primary antibodies included: anti-FTMT (ab124889, Abcam), anti-Mfrn1 (PA5-26720, Invitrogen), anti-Mfrn2 (PA5-42498, Invitrogen); anti-ACTB (AC-15, Sigma) served as loading control. Bands were quantified in ImageJ, normalized to ACTB, and analyzed in GraphPad Prism 9 (unpaired  t -test; significance thresholds: ∗ P  < 0.05, ∗∗ P  < 0.01, ∗∗∗ P  < 0.001; n.s., not significant).    2.8  Primary rat embryonic fibroblasts (REFs) and treatments  REFs were derived from E13–15 embryos by standard protocols [ 28 ]. Genotypes and sex were determined by PCR [ 15 , 29 ]. Male-derived WT and Brca1-MUT REFs were maintained in DMEM (043-30085, Wako, Osaka, Japan) with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Biowest; Nuaillé, France) and Mito + Serum Extender (355006, Corning, USA). REFs were immortalized via lentiviral transduction of SV40 (Addgene#22298) packaged with pspAX2 (#12260) and VSV-G (#14888). For oxidative stress, cells were treated with Fe-NTA (500 μM, 6 h) prior to fixation.    2.9  Immunofluorescence (confocal)  Cells were fixed, permeabilized and stained with anti-TOM20 (11802-1-AP, Proteintech) and anti-γ-H2AX (05-636, Sigma-Aldrich); nuclei were counterstained with DAPI. A Zeiss confocal microscope (LSM880, Carl Zeiss) was applied for image acquisition.    2.10  Mitochondrial respiration  Oxygen consumption (OCR) and extracellular acidification (ECAR) were measured on a Seahorse XFe24 Analyzer (Agilent) following manufacture's instructions. Briefly, REFs were seeded (6 × 10 4 /well) in Seahorse XF DMEM (103575-100) supplemented with 10 mM glucose, 1 mM pyruvate, 2 mM glutamine (103577/8/9-100) on a Seahorse XFe24 plate and incubated overnight. The XF Cell Mito Stress Test Kit (103015-100) was run with sequential injections of oligomycin 1.5 μM, FCCP 1 μM, and rotenone/antimycin A 0.5 μM. Cell count was quantified using BioTek Cytation 5 and Keyence BZ-X800 for normalization. Data were processed per manufacturer's instructions and analyzed in GraphPad Prism 9 (unpaired  t -test with significance shown in  Fig. 8 E ).    2.11  TCGA transcriptomic cohorts  To evaluate the clinical relevance of karyomegaly-associated transcriptional programs identified in our experimental model, we analyzed data obtained from the TCGA Pan-Cancer Clinical Data Resource, for TCGA-KIRC as the primary validation cohort, and additional tumor types for exploratory analyses, including TCGA-BRCA, TCGA-COAD, TCGA-LIHC, TCGA-LUAD, and TCGA-LUSC [ 30 ].  RNA-seq data were retrieved via TCGAbiolinks v2.32.0 [ 31 ] from the NCI GDC. Tumor-adjacent solid tissue normal (STN) samples were used for the primary analyses, whereas primary tumor samples were evaluated separately for independent validation. Raw counts were normalized by the trimmed mean of M-values (TMM) method using edgeR v4.2.2 [ 32 ] and converted to log 2 -counts per million (log 2 -CPM; prior count = 1). For duplicate gene entries, the isoform with the highest mean expression was retained.   2.11.1  Karyomegalic module definition and scoring  Four gene modules were evaluated (Fig. S7A). Three gene modules were defined based on findings from our Xenium spatial transcriptomics data. Module activity was quantified by single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) using GSVA v1.52.3 [ 33 ], computed independently within each tissue compartment (STN or tumor). Only modules with at least three genes present in the expression matrix were retained. Patient-level scores were derived as mean across available samples.    2.11.2  Survival analysis  Clinical annotations, including progression-free interval (PFI) and overall survival (OS), were obtained from curated TCGA clinical datasets. For each module, patients were stratified into high- and low-score groups using the cohort-specific median module score as the cutoff. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were generated using the survival and survminer packages.  Associations between module activity and clinical outcome were evaluated using log-rank tests and univariable Cox proportional hazards models. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated from Cox models. Analyses were performed separately for PFI and OS endpoints. Cohorts with fewer than five outcome events or insufficient matched samples were excluded from survival testing.  A tiered strategy was used for Multiple-testing correction. We designated TCGA-KIRC as the confirmatory cohort and analyzed non-renal cancer cohorts in an exploratory manner. Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction was therefore performed separately within confirmatory and exploratory tiers. Statistical significance was assessed primarily using the tier-specific FDR-adjusted results.    2.11.3  BRCA1 mutation carrier and control definition  BRCA1 germline carriers were defined as described [ 34 ]. Non-carrier controls were identified by a two-tiered exclusion strategy requiring availability of diagnostic WSIs and absence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic germline variants in BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, RAD51C, RAD51D, BARD1, and NBN. Controls were further selected by two-stage propensity score matching to control for clinical covariates [ 35 ] .  The final cohort comprised 20 BRCA1 germline carriers and 63 matched non-carrier controls (76.2% ductal, 4.8% lobular, 19.0% other histological subtypes).    2.11.4  Histopathological image analysis  Diagnostic whole slide images (WSIs) for TCGA-BRCA were obtained from the NCI Genomic Data Commons (GDC). Germline variant data were accessed from the TCGA PanCanAtlas Germline dataset [ 34 ] under controlled GDC access (dbGaP: phs000178), in compliance with the TCGA data use agreement.  Regions of interest (ROIs) containing well-formed ductal tubules were manually annotated in ductal carcinoma WSIs from both groups using QuPath v0.4 [ 36 ] (15 controls, 7 carriers; ROI count was limited by preserved adjacent normal portions). Nucleus segmentation was performed using Cellpose v2.3.2 [ 37 ], and morphological features were extracted using scikit-image. A post-hoc quality filter was applied to remove spurious detections. Nucleus-level analyses are presented as exploratory findings; patient-level analyses constitute the primary statistical inference.      3  Results   3.1  Xenium in situ on early stages of Fe-NTA-induced renal carcinogenesis  To identify early alterations during iron-driven renal carcinogenesis, we analyzed kidneys from wild-type (WT) and  Brca1  mutant ( L63X/+ ; MUT) rats subjected to Fe-NTA administration, as previously described [ 15 ]. Because rat-compatible spatial transcriptomic panels remain limited, we designed a custom 50-gene Xenium panel covering renal structural markers from single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets [ 21 ], together with genes related to iron metabolism, mitochondrial function, and tumorigenesis based on our previous studies [ 5 , 38 ].  Six kidney samples representing control, 1-week, and 3-week Fe-NTA exposure in WT and MUT rats were analyzed across two Xenium slides. DAPI-based segmentation captured approximately 324,765–531,476 cells per sample, with median transcript detection of 62–104 transcripts per cell ( Fig. 1 A). Post-Xenium H&E staining preserved tissue morphology and enabled direct integration of spatial transcriptomics with histopathology ( Fig. 1 A–D). Seurat-based clustering identified 53 cellular clusters, which were annotated into 10 major renal cell categories based on marker expression and histological context ( Fig. 1 B and C;  Fig. S1A and B ). Molecular annotations closely matched H&E-defined structures, supporting robust cell-type assignment even with a focused gene panel ( Fig. 1 D). Cluster composition varied across genotype and treatment conditions, with prominent changes in proximal tubules and stromal cells ( Fig. S1C ), indicating early remodeling of epithelial and interstitial compartments during Fe-NTA-induced carcinogenesis.    3.2  Characterization of key-gene signatures in early renal carcinogenesis  We next focused on transcriptional remodeling of proximal tubular cells (PTs), the principal target of Fe-NTA-induced renal carcinogenesis. Refined clustering of PT and stromal compartments improved resolution of treatment- and genotype-associated cell states ( Fig. S2A and B ). Single-cell expression analysis revealed reciprocal regulation of homeostatic and injury-associated genes in PTs ( Fig. 2 A). In control kidneys, PTs highly expressed renal function and mitochondrial metabolism genes, hereafter referred to as “friend key-genes,” including  Lrp2, Pink1,  and  Amacr . In contrast, Fe-NTA exposure induced “foe key-genes” associated with injury and tumorigenesis, including  Myc, Met, Lcn2 , and  Anxa2 , with concomitant reduction of homeostatic markers.  Several foe key-genes were induced as early as 1 week after Fe-NTA exposure in both genotypes ( Fig. 2 A). Although  Met, Anxa2, Lcn2, Sfxn3 , and  Klf4  showed partial reduction by 3 weeks,  Myc  and  Slc22a17  remained elevated or further increased. At 3 weeks, MUT PTs showed stronger expression of foe markers than WT, whereas  Lrp2  and  Amacr  were more strongly reduced, indicating genotype-dependent epithelial remodeling under oxidative stress. Spatial mapping with Giotto confirmed that friend key-genes were enriched in intact tubular segments, whereas foe key-genes localized to histologically abnormal regions with tubular dilation, disruption, or loss of recognizable tubular organization ( Fig. 2 C).  Because karyomegalic PTs are a characteristic lesion in Fe-NTA-treated kidneys [ 39 , 40 ], we quantified nuclear morphology using Xenium-derived nuclear polygons ( Fig. 2 B). Fe-NTA exposure was associated with nuclear enlargement, reduced compactness and circularity, and increased eccentricity. WT karyomegalic cells had larger nuclei than MUT cells under comparable treatment conditions ( Fig. S5A ). These data indicate that nuclear remodeling accompanies early Fe-NTA-induced epithelial injury and is modified by Brca1 haploinsufficiency.    3.3  Dynamics of diverse PT subtypes in early renal carcinogenesis  To resolve PT dynamics during early carcinogenesis, we reclustered PTs and identified 11 subtypes ( Fig. 3 A and B). Homeostatic PT clusters 1, 2, 5, 6, 10, and 12 predominated in control kidneys and expressed renal functional and mitochondrial genes. In contrast, clusters 0, 3, 4, 7, 8, and 9 emerged after Fe-NTA exposure and showed increased injury-, repair-, or foe key-gene expression with reduced homeostatic programs. Genotype-specific differences became evident after Fe-NTA exposure: WT kidneys showed transient loss of normal tubular states at 1 week with partial recovery by 3 weeks, whereas MUT kidneys showed expansion of injured clusters, particularly clusters 4 and 7.  The PT subtypes represented distinct biological states ( Fig. 3 B). Oxidative Stress–Adaptive PTs (cluster 0; OA_PT) expressed antioxidant and metabolic genes such as  Cubn, Slc40a1, Lrp2, Slc27a2 , and  Gpx4 , together with moderate  Myc  and  Met  expression. DNA Damage–Response PTs (cluster 3; DR_PT) expressed repair and regenerative markers including  Mki67, Rad51, Bard1 , and  Bap1 . Maladaptive Repair PTs (clusters 4 and 7; MR_PT) expressed  Lcn2, Slc22a17 , and other foe key-genes, with cluster 4 retaining more friend key-gene expression than cluster 7. Transient Regenerative PTs (cluster 8; TR_PT) expressed proliferation and DNA repair markers, whereas Ferroptotic PTs (cluster 9; Fer_PT) were often isolated necrotic or pyknotic cells within otherwise preserved tubules, as confirmed by Xenium Explorer alignment with H&E images ( Fig. S3A ).  Spatially, DR_PT localized mainly near the cortex–medulla boundary in WT kidneys at 1 week but was less evident in MUT kidneys ( Fig. 3 C). MR_PT populations frequently co-localized within MUT tubules, whereas WT tubules showed greater admixture of homeostatic, oxidative stress–adaptive, and transient regenerative states. Stromal reclustering further identified 13 stromal subtypes with genotype- and treatment-dependent composition ( Fig. 3 D). After 3 weeks of Fe-NTA, MUT kidneys showed expansion of stromal states enriched for regenerative, injury-response, iron-handling, matrix-remodeling, and macrophage-recruiting signatures, including ST_1, ST_3, ST_5/8, ST_6, and ST_9.  To summarize PT status spatially, we generated pathology-informed module scores ( Fig. S3B–D ). Spatial score maps showed that normal tubular scores declined after 1 week of Fe-NTA exposure and partially recovered in WT kidneys by 3 weeks, whereas MUT kidneys showed more persistent dysfunction ( Fig. 3 E). Interestingly, scores representing renal injury and cell death (acute/subacute injured score; dying tubules score) displayed inverse spatial patterns to normal tubules score at 1-week Fe-NTA treatment, with reduced acute injured score at 3-week Fe-NTA treatment, marking the progression of homeostatic PT clusters toward subacute injury and the initiation of cellular adaptations linked to ferroptosis resistance and potential oncogenic transformation.    3.4  Nuclear morphometrics reflect transcriptional behaviors in pathological/genotype-dependent patterns  We next asked whether nuclear morphology captures transcriptional states at single-cell resolution. Morphological features derived from Xenium polygons included nuclear area, eccentricity, circularity, compactness, convexity, and solidity ( Fig. 4 A). Gene–morphology associations were quantified using covariate-adjusted linear models with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction. In Fe-NTA 3-week samples, morphology-associated coefficients revealed coordinated relationships between nuclear shape and PT transcriptional state ( Fig. 4 B). Oncogenic and iron-associated genes, including  Lcn2, Anxa2, Met, Pcbp2, Myc , and  Sfxn3,  were positively associated with eccentricity and convexity, whereas circular and compact nuclei were associated with preserved PT markers such as S lc27a2, Lrp2, Pink1,  and  Tfrc . Although the overall direction of associations was similar between WT and MUT kidneys, MUT showed stronger coefficients, indicating amplified coupling between nuclear morphology and stress-associated transcription under Brca1 haploinsufficiency.  We then converted morphology–gene β profiles into gene–gene networks using cosine similarity. Under the pre-specified criteria of FDR ≤0.05, β ≥ 0.10, and cosine ≥0.70, robust modules were absent in control kidneys and WT Fe-NTA 3-week kidneys, whereas WT Fe-NTA 1-week kidneys showed compact Slc27a2–Lrp2–Pink1 and Mki67–Anxa2 modules ( Fig. 4 C). In contrast, MUT kidneys retained modules at both 1 and 3 weeks, including a recurrent Slc27a2–Lrp2 core and an Lcn2–Anxa2 injury-associated core, suggesting genotype-dependent persistence of morphology-linked transcriptional programs.  To identify transcriptional correlates of nuclear chromatin organization during early carcinogenic nuclear transformation, we derived three nuclear morphometric parameters: hematoxylin optical density (HOD), nuclear substructure density (NSD) [ 41 ], and peripheral intensity index (PII) [ 42 ], from H&E images of WT and MUT Fe-NTA 3w kidneys. HOD provided quantitative readout of bulk nuclear chromatin compaction. In WT, the genes most strongly associated with HOD (e.g.,  Gpx4 ,  Fth1 ,  Ncoa4 ,  Pcbp1 , Tfrc) were uniformly negative, indicating that more robust iron-homeostatic programs correspond to lower nuclear hematoxylin density, consistent with a more open chromatin state ( Fig. 4 D;  Table S2 ). In MUT, PT identity genes (e.g.,  Amacr ,  Slc27a2 ,  Lrp2 ) again showed strong negative associations, whereas top positive associations were observed for  Sfxn3 ,  Sting1 ,  Mcub ,  S100a9 ,  Anxa2 , and  Lcn2 , suggesting that chromatin compaction is associated with mitochondrial alteration and stress responses in Brca1 deficient carcinogenesis. Despite that majority of significant genes were genotype-specific, effect direction was replicated across genotypes for  Lrp2 ,  Slc27a2 , and  Amacr  (negative in both) and for  Lgals1 ,  Anxa2 ,  Pcbp2 , and  Bard1  (positive in both). Fixed-effects meta-analysis was consistent with an overall pattern during oxidative stress-based carcinogenesis, where homeostatic genes downregulate with chromatin compaction, while carcinogenetic pathways across injury/iron-overload/fibrosis are activated, especially more pronounced in  BRCA1  mutants.  NSD [ 41 ], which detected hematoxylin-dense intranuclear foci, showed no detectable gene-level association in either genotype ( Fig. S4B ), consistent with its proposed role as constitutive, transcriptionally silent chromatin compartment (e.g., chromocenters). PII captured the distribution of peripheral heterochromatin (lamina-associated domains (LADs)), providing a complementary readout of nuclear architectural organization. In WT, PT metabolic genes (e.g.,  Pink1 ,  Slc27a2 ,  Tfrc ,  Fth1 ,  Gpx4 ,  Ncoa4 ,  Pcbp2 ) were positively associated with PII, indicating that they correspond to greater peripheral enrichment of condensed chromatin, consistent with intact LAD organization ( Fig. 4 E;  Table S2 ). In MUT,  Slc27a2 ,  Amacr , and  Lrp2  retained similar positive associations, while  Mcub ,  Sting1 , and  Cdkn1/2a  showed significant negative associations not observed in WT, implying a distinct transcriptional signature related to peripheral heterochromatin loss [ 43 , 44 ]. As with HOD, cross concordance was low overall, although  Slc27a2 ,  Gpx4 , and  Pink1  replicated a consistent positive direction in both genotypes. Meta-analysis identified positive pooled effects for PT/iron/mitochondrial metabolic genes (e.g.,  Lrp2 ,  Slc27a2 ,  Amacr ), alongside negative effects including  Cdkn1/2a ,  Mcub ,  Lcn2 ,  Myc , and  Lgals1  ( Fig. 4 E).  Together, these results indicate that HOD and PII both capture a shared transcriptional axis linking proximal tubule homeostasis to chromatin reorganization, with this signature more extensive in MUT. These findings also demonstrate that nuclear chromatin morphometry can be systematically linked to spatial transcriptomic profiles, identifying candidate chromatin-state markers of early renal carcinogenesis.    3.5  Epithelial karyomegaly classified into subtypes with distinct biological signatures  We defined karyomegalic epithelial cells as PTs with nuclear area greater than mean + 2SD and elongated cells as those with axis ratio >2. Compared with other PTs, enlarged nuclei showed consistent  Cdkn1a  upregulation and  Pink1  downregulation, with heterogeneous induction of DNA damage repair and regenerative genes ( Fig. 5 A;  Fig. S5C and D ). Elongated cells showed impaired epithelial function with increased  Sfxn3  and modest  Rad51  and  Mki67  induction ( Fig. S5B ). Because karyomegalic cells showed clear transcriptional heterogeneity and group-dependent differences in incidence, we focused subsequent analyses on enlarged epithelial nuclei. We next investigated the morphological and transcriptional features of re-clustered karyomegalic subpopulations. Among all clusters, K1 displayed the most pronounced nuclear enlargement with irregular, rough nuclear contours, and thus most closely aligned with the canonical pathological definition of karyomegaly ( Fig. 5 B, D). Transcriptional profiling further revealed strong induction of  Cdkn1a , coordinated with elevated  Ncoa4  and reduced  Fth1 , indicative of stress-associated cell-cycle arrest with an active ferritinophagy-mediated iron-mobilization program ( Fig. 5 C, S5E). K4 was enriched for markers of proximal tubule homeostasis and metabolic competence (e.g.,  Lrp2, Slc27a2, Amacr, Pink1 ), suggesting maintenance of epithelial transport and mitochondrial quality control in WT ( Fig. 5 B, C). And in morphological perspectives, K4 showed relatively more solid and compact nucleus. Strikingly, K2 and K5 co-expressed  Met, Lcn2,  and  Myc , pointing to an adaptive stress program with oncogenic features, whereas significant nuclear morphology features included elongation yet smaller area than K1. We interpret these states as a potential early pro-tumorigenic niche in BRCA1-haploinsufficient kidneys that may represent an actionable window for intervention in carcinogenesis.  To determine whether karyomegaly represents not only an altered epithelial state but also a local epithelial microenvironment, we profiled PT neighbors located within 30 μm of either karyomegalic or non-karyomegalic PT cells. PTs adjacent to karyomegalic cells showed increased expression of iron-handling, oxidative stress–adaptive, and pro-survival genes, including  Lcn2, Anxa2, Mki67, Sfxn3, Cdkn1a,  and  Myc , together with reduced  Amacr, Aqp3,  and  Pink1  ( Fig. 5 E). These signatures partially mirrored those of karyomegalic cells themselves, indicating that surrounding epithelial cells acquire a stress-adapted, survival-biased state. This interpretation is supported by the induction of factors linked to ferroptotic vulnerability, including  Lcn2 , which can modulate labile iron availability and antioxidant defenses [ 45 ], and by reduced  Pink1 , suggesting impaired mitophagy [ 46 ].  Subtype-stratified analysis further showed that PTs surrounding K2 cells were enriched for  Myc, Lcn2, Slc40a1,  and  Met , with reduced  Amacr, Pink1,  and  Slc27a2,  whereas PTs surrounding K4 cells maintained metabolic and mitochondrial homeostasis genes ( Fig. 5 E). Thus, karyomegalic states appear to act as focal organizers of local epithelial programs, with BRCA1-haploinsufficient karyomegaly defining a stress-adaptive, iron-handling, proto-oncogenic niche permissive for iron-driven carcinogenesis.    3.6  Stromal neighbors contribute to distinct regulatory system in BRCA1-MUT kidneys  Because renal epithelial injury occurs within an integrated tubulointerstitial environment [ 47 , 48 ], we examined stromal proximity and microenvironmental organization.
